title: Sampling and Uncertainty
section: Why This Matters for Your Final Project
text:
Why This Matters for Your Final Project

Your Research Design is due March 18
You will need to describe where your data comes from and why your sample is appropriate
After today, you’ll be able to read and explain every number in your regression output

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text: November 3, 1948

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
What Went Wrong?
The pollsters were certain Dewey would win.


Gallup, Roper, and Crossley all predicted a comfortable Dewey victory
They used quota sampling: interviewers chose respondents matching demographic quotas
But interviewers gravitated toward wealthier, more accessible, more Republican-leaning people
The sample was big. That was not the problem.
The problem was who was in it and who was not.

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
The Lesson


The polls missed a late swing to Truman among undecided voters
The samples systematically over-represented one type of voter
A big sample does not fix a biased sample
This is the first rule: before you trust any number, ask where the data came from

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
Today’s Plan



Is your sample any good? (Representativeness)
Even with a good sample, different samples give different answers (Sampling variability)
How do we account for that noise? (Standard errors, confidence intervals)
The same logic applies to experiments and regressions (Inference)


Your Research Design is due March 18. After today you will be able to describe your data, justify your sample, and interpret every number in a regression table.

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
Before You Do Anything Else


Think about your sample.



Who is in it?
Who is left out?
Why?

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
The Takeaway




A bad sample will give you a wrong answer no matter how sophisticated your statistics are
A big sample does not fix a biased sample (Dewey’s pollsters had thousands of respondents)
Random sampling is the gold standard because everyone has a known chance of being selected
ALWAYS interrogate your sample before you interpret results

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
A Running Example


Say we want to know the average height of Penn students.

There are about 25,000 students. We cannot measure all of them. So we grab 50 students at random.


For the sake of this simulation, let’s pretend we know the true average is 67.5 inches (about 5’8”).

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
You Sample 50 Students


Show code
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(42)

# True population of Penn students
pop_size <- 25000
pop_height <- rnorm(pop_size, mean = 67.5, sd = 3.5)
true_mean <- mean(pop_height)

# Draw ONE sample of 50
one_sample <- sample(pop_height, 50)

ggplot(data.frame(x = one_sample), aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "#011F5B", alpha = 0.7, bins = 20, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(one_sample), color = "#011F5B", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_mean, color = "red", linewidth = 1.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("label", x = mean(one_sample) + 2, y = 8,
           label = paste0("Sample mean = ", round(mean(one_sample), 1), " in"),
           color = "#011F5B", size = 5) +
  annotate("label", x = true_mean - 2, y = 8,
           label = paste0("True mean = ", round(true_mean, 1), " in"),
           color = "red", size = 5) +
  labs(x = "Height (inches)", y = "Count",
       title = "One random sample of 50 Penn students") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18)

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
Your Friend Samples 50 Different Students
Neither of you did anything wrong. You both sampled randomly. But you grabbed different people, so you got a different answer.


Show code
set.seed(99)
friend_sample <- sample(pop_height, 50)

both <- rbind(
  data.frame(height = one_sample,
             who = paste0("Your sample (mean = ",
                          round(mean(one_sample), 1), " in)")),
  data.frame(height = friend_sample,
             who = paste0("Friend's sample (mean = ",
                          round(mean(friend_sample), 1), " in)"))
)

ggplot(both, aes(x = height)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "#011F5B", alpha = 0.7, bins = 20, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_mean, color = "red", linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~who, ncol = 1) +
  annotate("label", x = true_mean, y = Inf, vjust = 2,
           label = paste0("True mean = ", round(true_mean, 1), " in"),
           color = "red", size = 4) +
  labs(x = "Height (inches)", y = "Count",
       title = "Same population, different samples, different answers") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
section: What If 1,000 People Each Sampled 50 Students?
text:
What If 1,000 People Each Sampled 50 Students?


Show code
set.seed(42)
n_sims <- 1000
sample_means <- numeric(n_sims)

for (i in 1:n_sims) {
  sample_means[i] <- mean(sample(pop_height, 50))
}

ggplot(data.frame(means = sample_means), aes(x = means)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "#011F5B", alpha = 0.7, bins = 30, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_mean, color = "red", linewidth = 1.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("label", x = true_mean, y = 90,
           label = paste0("True mean = ", round(true_mean, 1), " in"),
           color = "red", size = 6) +
  labs(x = "Sample mean (inches)", y = "Count",
       title = "1,000 sample means from 1,000 different samples of 50 students") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18)

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
The Standard Error
Any single estimate is still off by a little. How much?

The standard error (SE) is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution.




It tells you: how much does my estimate bounce around across repeated samples?
Small SE = precise (narrow distribution)
Large SE = imprecise (wide distribution)
Bigger sample = smaller SE

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
Bigger Samples, Less Wiggle


Show code
set.seed(42)

means_30 <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(pop_height, 30)))
means_200 <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(pop_height, 200)))

compare <- rbind(
  data.frame(mean_height = means_30,
             sample = paste0("n = 30  (SE = ", round(sd(means_30), 2), " in)")),
  data.frame(mean_height = means_200,
             sample = paste0("n = 200  (SE = ", round(sd(means_200), 2), " in)"))
)

ggplot(compare, aes(x = mean_height)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "#011F5B", alpha = 0.7, bins = 30, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_mean, color = "red", linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~sample, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Sample mean (inches)", y = "Count",
       title = "More data, less wiggle") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
This Is What Polls Report


When a poll says “52% support Candidate A, plus or minus 3 percentage points”…



The 52% is their sample estimate
The +/- 3 is the margin of error (roughly 1.96 times the standard error)
They are saying: if we polled a different random sample of voters, the answer would probably land somewhere between 49% and 55%




This is a confidence interval.

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
Seeing It in Action
Each line is a 95% CI from a different sample. The red dashed line is the truth.


Show code
set.seed(42)
n_sims <- 100
results <- data.frame(
  sim = 1:n_sims,
  mean_hat = numeric(n_sims),
  se = numeric(n_sims)
)

for (i in 1:n_sims) {
  s <- sample(pop_height, 50)
  results$mean_hat[i] <- mean(s)
  results$se[i] <- sd(s) / sqrt(50)
}

results$lower <- results$mean_hat - 1.96 * results$se
results$upper <- results$mean_hat + 1.96 * results$se
results$covers <- results$lower <= true_mean & results$upper >= true_mean
coverage <- round(mean(results$covers) * 100)

ggplot(results, aes(x = sim, y = mean_hat, color = covers)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = true_mean, color = "red", linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "orange", "TRUE" = "#011F5B"),
                     labels = c("Misses the truth", "Contains the truth")) +
  labs(x = "Sample number", y = "Estimated mean height (in)",
       title = paste0(coverage, " out of 100 confidence intervals contain the true mean"),
       color = "") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
From Means to Treatment Effects


So far: if you sample 50 students and compute the average height, a different sample gives a slightly different average. That is sampling variability.

Now imagine you run an experiment. You randomly assign people to treatment and control, measure the outcome, and estimate the treatment effect.


Same thing. A different random assignment, or a different sample of participants, would give you a slightly different estimate of the effect.

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
A Quick Simulation


Show code
set.seed(42)
true_effect <- 3  # true treatment effect: 3 points on a test

n_sims <- 1000
effects <- numeric(n_sims)

for (i in 1:n_sims) {
  treat <- rnorm(50, mean = 75 + true_effect, sd = 10)
  control <- rnorm(50, mean = 75, sd = 10)
  effects[i] <- mean(treat) - mean(control)
}

ggplot(data.frame(effect = effects), aes(x = effect)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "#011F5B", alpha = 0.7, bins = 30, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_effect, color = "red", linewidth = 1.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("label", x = true_effect, y = 90,
           label = paste0("True effect = ", true_effect),
           color = "red", size = 6) +
  labs(x = "Estimated treatment effect", y = "Count",
       title = "1,000 experiments, each with 100 participants",
       subtitle = "Same true effect, different estimates every time") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18)

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
section: So How Do We Know if an Effect Is Real?
text:
So How Do We Know if an Effect Is Real?


The question becomes: is my estimate far enough from zero that it probably is not just noise?


Null hypothesis (\(H_0\)): there is no effect. The true parameter is zero.


The p-value: if there were truly no effect, how surprising would my estimate be?




Small p-value (< 0.05): this would be very surprising under no effect → reject the null
Large p-value (> 0.05): this is consistent with no effect → fail to reject the null

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
The Stars





Symbol
p-value
Meaning




***
< 0.001
Very strong evidence against \(H_0\)


**
< 0.01
Strong evidence


*
< 0.05
Evidence


.
< 0.1
Weak evidence


(none)
> 0.1
Not statistically significant




The 0.05 threshold is a convention, not a law of nature.

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
Reading summary(lm())
We have been working with height. Now let’s see this in a regression. We simulate data where each additional inch of height adds ~0.4 points to a basketball tryout score.

options(scipen = 999)

set.seed(42)
tryout <- data.frame(
  height = round(sample(pop_height, 80), 1)
)
tryout$score <- 40 + 0.4 * tryout$height + rnorm(80, 0, 5)

model <- lm(score ~ height, data = tryout)
summary(model)


Call:
lm(formula = score ~ height, data = tryout)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-14.836  -3.067   0.504   3.273  13.627 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value    Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  39.2662     7.1884   5.462 0.000000542 ***
height        0.4092     0.1064   3.845    0.000244 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 4.895 on 78 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1594,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1486 
F-statistic: 14.79 on 1 and 78 DF,  p-value: 0.0002445

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
Confidence Interval in R

confint(model)

                 2.5 %     97.5 %
(Intercept) 24.9551596 53.5772870
height       0.1973415  0.6210762




The 95% CI for the effect of height is [0.2, 0.62].


Does not contain zero, consistent with the small p-value: we have evidence that taller students score higher on the tryout.

Before You Trust a Result




Is the sample representative of the population you care about?
Are the standard errors small relative to the coefficient?
Does the confidence interval exclude zero?
Does the result make substantive sense?




Statistics cannot save you from a bad sample or a bad research design.

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
The Big Question


Most of the time in research, we want to say something about a population.


What is the average income in Nigeria?
Does a new vaccine reduce child mortality?
Do term limits reduce corruption?



But we almost never observe the whole population. We observe a sample.


So: how do we make claims about the population from a sample?

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
Before Anything Else


Before you run a single regression, before you compute a single mean, you need to ask:



Who is in my sample?
Who is left out?
Why?




If the answer to “who is left out” is “people who are systematically different from the rest,” you have a problem. And no amount of statistics will fix it.

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
section: How Sampling Goes Wrong in Practice
text:
How Sampling Goes Wrong in Practice



Even with good intentions, samples can be systematically off:




Survey only urban areas: miss rural poverty
Phone surveys: miss people without phones
Only villages near roads: miss remote populations
Household surveys: miss homeless, displaced, migrant populations
Voluntary response: people with strong opinions over-represented

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
section: OK, But What If Your Sample Is Good?
text:
OK, But What If Your Sample Is Good?


Say you did everything right. Random sampling, good coverage, representative.

Are you done worrying?


No. Because even a perfectly representative sample introduces another kind of uncertainty.

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
You Already Know This Intuitively


When a poll says “52% support Candidate A, plus or minus 3 percentage points”…



The 52% is their sample estimate
The +/- 3 is the margin of error (roughly 1.96 times the standard error)
They are saying: if we polled a different random sample of voters, the answer would probably land between 49% and 55%




That range is a confidence interval.

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
section: How to Interpret a Confidence Interval
text:
How to Interpret a Confidence Interval


The correct interpretation:
If we repeated this study many times, each time drawing a new sample and computing a new CI, about 95% of those intervals would contain the true value.

The common but WRONG interpretation:
“There is a 95% probability that the true value is in this interval.”


Why is that wrong? Because the true value is fixed. It is either in the interval or it is not. The interval is the thing that changes from sample to sample.

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
From Averages to Treatment Effects


Everything we just did was about estimating a mean. Different sample, different mean, standard error tells you how much it wiggles.

Now think about causal research. You run an experiment: randomly assign people to treatment and control, measure the outcome, estimate the treatment effect.


Same problem. If you had recruited slightly different participants, or randomized differently, you would get a slightly different estimate of the effect. The true effect is the same, but your estimate has noise.

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
section: We Could Repeat a Million Times…
text:
We Could Repeat a Million Times…


In theory, if we could run the same experiment a million times with different samples, we would get a million estimates. The distribution of those estimates would be a bell curve centered on the true effect.

Let’s pretend we can do that:

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
Simulating 1,000 Experiments


Show code
set.seed(42)
true_effect <- 5  # true effect: 5 points on a test

n_sims <- 1000
effects <- numeric(n_sims)

for (i in 1:n_sims) {
  treat <- rnorm(40, mean = 70 + true_effect, sd = 12)
  control <- rnorm(40, mean = 70, sd = 12)
  effects[i] <- mean(treat) - mean(control)
}

ggplot(data.frame(effect = effects), aes(x = effect)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "#011F5B", alpha = 0.7, bins = 30, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_effect, color = "red", linewidth = 1.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("label", x = true_effect + 1, y = 85,
           label = paste0("True effect = ", true_effect, " points"),
           color = "red", size = 5, hjust = 0) +
  labs(x = "Estimated treatment effect (points)", y = "Count",
       title = "1,000 experiments, same true effect, different estimates") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18)

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
…But We Cannot


In real life, you run your experiment once. You get one estimate.

You cannot repeat it a million times. So how do you know whether your one estimate is close to the truth or far from it?


This is the problem of statistical inference: using your one sample to say something about what would happen if you could repeat the study.


The tools are the same: standard errors tell you how much the estimate would wiggle, and confidence intervals give you a plausible range.

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
section: But There Is a Harder Question
text:
But There Is a Harder Question


When we were estimating average height, we just wanted to know “how close is our estimate to the truth?”

With treatment effects, we have a sharper question: is the effect actually there at all, or is it just noise?



Null hypothesis (\(H_0\)): there is no effect. The true parameter is zero.


The p-value: if there were truly no effect, how surprising would our estimate be?

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
The Checklist


Before you trust any result:


Is the sample representative of the population you care about?
Is the standard error small relative to the estimate?
Does the confidence interval exclude zero (or whatever value matters)?
Does the result make substantive sense?




Good statistics cannot save a bad sample or a bad research design.

Know your sample
Getting it right on average
Quantifying how off you are

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
section: Your Data Can Only Speak to What Is In It
text:
Your Data Can Only Speak to What Is In It


Before you run a single analysis, ask:


What is my unit of observation?
What units are in my sample?
What units are left out?



Your data cannot tell you anything about anything else!

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
This Happens in Research Too


Survey only urban areas: miss rural poverty
Phone surveys: miss people without phones
Only villages near roads: miss remote populations
Household surveys: miss homeless, displaced, migrant populations
Voluntary response: people with strong opinions over-represented

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
The Setup


Say we want to know the average height of Penn students.

There are about 25,000 students. We cannot measure all of them. So we grab 30 at random.


For this simulation, let’s pretend we know the true average is 67.5 inches (about 5’8”).

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
One Sample of 30 Students


Show code
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(42)

# True population of Penn students
pop_size <- 25000
pop_height <- rnorm(pop_size, mean = 67.5, sd = 5)
true_mean <- mean(pop_height)

# Draw ONE sample of 30
one_sample <- sample(pop_height, 30)

ggplot(data.frame(x = one_sample), aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "#011F5B", alpha = 0.7, bins = 15, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(one_sample), color = "#011F5B", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_mean, color = "red", linewidth = 1.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("label", x = mean(one_sample) + 2.5, y = 5,
           label = paste0("Sample mean = ", round(mean(one_sample), 1), " in"),
           color = "#011F5B", size = 5) +
  annotate("label", x = true_mean - 2.5, y = 5,
           label = paste0("True mean = ", round(true_mean, 1), " in"),
           color = "red", size = 5) +
  labs(x = "Height (inches)", y = "Count",
       title = "One random sample of 30 Penn students") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18)

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
Grab Another Sample
Same population. Another 30 students, chosen at random. Different answer.


Show code
set.seed(99)
second_sample <- sample(pop_height, 30)

both <- rbind(
  data.frame(height = one_sample,
             which = paste0("Sample 1 (mean = ",
                          round(mean(one_sample), 1), " in)")),
  data.frame(height = second_sample,
             which = paste0("Sample 2 (mean = ",
                          round(mean(second_sample), 1), " in)"))
)

  geom_histogram(fill = "#011F5B", alpha = 0.7, bins = 15, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_mean, color = "red", linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~which, ncol = 1) +
  annotate("label", x = true_mean, y = Inf, vjust = 2,
           label = paste0("True mean = ", round(true_mean, 1), " in"),

       title = "Same population, two different random samples") +

text:
Now Do This 1,000 Times


Show code
set.seed(42)
n_sims <- 1000
sample_means <- numeric(n_sims)

for (i in 1:n_sims) {
  sample_means[i] <- mean(sample(pop_height, 30))
}

  geom_histogram(fill = "#011F5B", alpha = 0.7, bins = 30, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_mean, color = "red", linewidth = 1.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("label", x = true_mean, y = 80,
           label = paste0("True mean = ", round(true_mean, 1), " in"),
           color = "red", size = 6) +

       title = "1,000 sample means, each from a different sample of 30") +

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
The Sampling Distribution




Every sample gives a slightly different answer
But the answers cluster around the truth
You never observe this distribution in real life. You only have your one sample.
But you know this distribution is approximately normal. That is the Central Limit Theorem.
And you can estimate how wide it is.

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
From Point Estimates to Ranges


Your point estimate is a little off each time. You saw this: every sample gives a slightly different mean.

So instead of reporting just one number, we report a range: the confidence interval.


\[CI = \text{estimate} \pm 1.96 \times SE\]


A 95% confidence interval is constructed so that, across repeated samples, 95% of such intervals will contain the true value.

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
section: The Same Logic for Treatment Effects
text:
The Same Logic for Treatment Effects


In research, we often do not just want to estimate a mean. We want to know whether some treatment or policy has an effect.

Same problem: if you ran the experiment with a slightly different sample, you would get a slightly different estimate of the effect. There is noise.


The question becomes: is the effect different from zero, or is it just noise?

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
section: But You Only Run It Once
text:
But You Only Run It Once


In real life, you run your experiment once. You get one estimate. You cannot repeat it a thousand times to see where the truth is.

That is what inference is: using your one sample to reason about what would happen across many samples. The SE and CI are your tools.



Null hypothesis (\(H_0\)): there is no effect. The true parameter is zero.


The p-value: if the true effect were zero, what is the probability of seeing an estimate at least as extreme as yours?

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
section: Is the Effect Different from Zero?
text:
Is the Effect Different from Zero?



Null hypothesis (\(H_0\)): there is no effect. The true parameter is zero.


The p-value: if there were truly no effect, what is the probability of seeing an estimate at least as extreme as yours?




Small p-value (< 0.05): very unlikely under no effect. Reject the null.
Large p-value (> 0.05): consistent with no effect. Fail to reject.

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
Every Number, Explained




Estimate (height): for each additional inch of height, tryout score increases by ~0.4 points
Std. Error: across repeated samples, this estimate would bounce around by about this much
t value: Estimate / Std. Error. How many SEs away from zero?
Pr(>|t|): the p-value. Would this be surprising if the true slope were zero?

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
section: On Average, We Get It Right
text:
On Average, We Get It Right


Two things:


Is this the right population? That is your call as a researcher. If you sampled Penn students, your mean tells you about Penn students. Not Drexel, not Temple. The sample mean is always right for the population you sampled from.
Given that population, your sample mean will on average equal the population value. And the distribution of sample means, if you took a million samples, would be normal. This is the Central Limit Theorem.



But any single estimate is still off by a little. How much?

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
Bigger Sample, Less Wiggle


Show code
set.seed(42)

means_30 <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(pop_height, 30)))
means_200 <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(pop_height, 200)))

compare <- rbind(
  data.frame(mean_height = means_30,
             sample = paste0("n = 30  (SE = ", round(sd(means_30), 2), " in)")),
  data.frame(mean_height = means_200,
             sample = paste0("n = 200  (SE = ", round(sd(means_200), 2), " in)"))
)

ggplot(compare, aes(x = mean_height)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "#011F5B", alpha = 0.7, bins = 30, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_mean, color = "red", linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~sample, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Sample mean (inches)", y = "Count",
       title = "More data, less wiggle") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
100 Confidence Intervals


Show code
set.seed(42)
n_sims <- 100
results <- data.frame(
  sim = 1:n_sims,
  mean_hat = numeric(n_sims),
  se = numeric(n_sims)
)

for (i in 1:n_sims) {
  s <- sample(pop_height, 30)
  results$mean_hat[i] <- mean(s)
  results$se[i] <- sd(s) / sqrt(30)
}

results$lower <- results$mean_hat - 1.96 * results$se
results$upper <- results$mean_hat + 1.96 * results$se
results$covers <- results$lower <= true_mean & results$upper >= true_mean
coverage <- round(mean(results$covers) * 100)

ggplot(results, aes(x = sim, y = mean_hat, color = covers)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = true_mean, color = "red", linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "orange", "TRUE" = "#011F5B"),
                     labels = c("Misses the truth", "Contains the truth")) +
  labs(x = "Sample number", y = "Estimated mean height (in)",
       title = paste0(coverage, " out of 100 intervals contain the true mean"),
       color = "") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
Same Logic for Treatment Effects


In research, we often care about whether some treatment has an effect, not just what the average is. Same problem: different sample, slightly different estimate, noise.

The question is usually: is the effect different from zero, or is it just noise?


To answer this, we imagine a world where there is no effect (the null hypothesis, \(H_0\)). Under that assumption, the sampling distribution of our estimate is centered at zero. How far out does our estimate land?

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
The Central Limit Theorem




The sample means center on the population value
And their distribution is normal
You never see this distribution in real life. You only have your one sample. But you know it is there and it is normal.
Why do we care that it is normal? Because we know everything about normal distributions. We can calculate exactly how spread out it is, where 95% of values fall, etc. That lets us quantify uncertainty.

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
The p-value
If the true effect were zero, this is what the sampling distribution would look like. The further out our estimate lands, the less likely it could have arisen by chance.

title: Sampling and Uncertainty
text:
p-values in Practice




Small p-value (< 0.05): very unlikely under no effect. Reject the null.
Large p-value (> 0.05): consistent with no effect. Fail to reject.
We usually set the threshold at 0.05, but it could be anything. It is a convention, not a law of nature.

Health and Development

Regression Discontinuity Design

title: Health and Development
text:
The State Provides Public Goods
Last week: the state and security

Crime can mobilize citizens (Bateson)
But policing can alienate them (Weaver and Lerman)


Today: the state and health

Governments build hospitals, subsidize medicine, regulate pollution
But development policies can also harm health

title: Health and Development
section: Are Development and Health Complements or Substitutes?
text:
Are Development and Health Complements or Substitutes?




Complements: economic growth → better nutrition, sanitation, medicine → longer lives
Substitutes: economic growth → pollution, industrial hazards, environmental degradation → shorter lives
Which one dominates depends on policy choices



Today’s paper: a case where a development policy had devastating health consequences

title: Health and Development
text:
The State of the World
Air quality in China is notoriously poor


Between 1981–2001, particulate concentrations were more than double China’s national standard and five times the level in the pre-1970 US
Premier Zhu Rongji (1999): “If I work in your Beijing, I would shorten my life at least five years”
Was he right?

title: Health and Development
text:
The Huai River Policy
During the 1950–1980 period of central planning, the Chinese government gave free coal winter heating

But due to budgetary constraints, this right was only extended to areas north of the Huai River.

title: Health and Development
text:
The Huai River





Cities north of the solid line were covered by the heating policy.

title: Health and Development
text:
The Research Question
Does sustained exposure to air pollution reduce life expectancy?



Pollution correlates with everything: income, urbanization, industry, access to healthcare
A simple comparison of polluted vs. clean areas confounds pollution with all of these
The Huai River policy creates a plausible natural quasi-experiment
Why?

title: Health and Development
text:
The Mechanism
Coal combustion releases Total Suspended Particulates (TSPs) into the air


TSPs penetrate the lungs and enter the bloodstream
Cause heart disease, stroke, lung cancer, respiratory illness
The medical evidence linking particulates to mortality is well established
The question is: how large is the effect at population scale?

title: Health and Development
text:
Data and Measurement
Air pollution: TSP concentrations from 90 cities (1981–2000)
Health: Mortality data from China’s Disease Surveillance Points (DSPs)

145 locations, nationally representative
Records all deaths and population counts
~500,000 recorded deaths between 1991 and 2000


**Treatment: north or south of the Huai River

title: Health and Development
text:
What Is a Regression Discontinuity?
Imagine you want to know: does passing a class improve your career?


Someone who scored 0 and someone who scored 100 are very different people
Comparing them confounds ability with passing
But what about someone who scored 59 vs. someone who scored 61?
Almost the same student. A bit of luck, random noise, one extra question
The only difference: one passed, the other did not

title: Health and Development
text:
RDD: The Intuition




Compare outcomes for units just above and just below the cutoff
If there is a jump in the outcome at the cutoff, that jump is the causal effect of treatment
Key assumption: nothing else changes discontinuously at the cutoff
It is like a local experiment around the cutoff

title: Health and Development
text:
The Chen et al. Design
\[TSP_j = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 North_j + \alpha_2 f(L_j) + X_j \kappa + \nu_j\]
\[Y_j = \delta_0 + \delta_1 North_j + \delta_2 f(L_j) + X_j \phi + u_j\]


\(j\): city
\(North_j\): indicator for being north of the Huai River
\(f(L_j)\): flexible polynomial in degrees of latitude from the river
\(X_j\): demographic and climate controls
\(\delta_1\): the discontinuous change in health at the river — what we want

title: Health and Development
text:
Does the Identifying Assumption Hold?


For this to work, nothing else should jump at the Huai River.


Education, income, urbanization, share with tap water: no discontinuity
Temperature, heating/cooling days: large differences, but smooth after adjusting for latitude
The Huai River is not an administrative boundary — it cuts through provinces
Predicted life expectancy (from covariates only, excluding pollution): no discontinuity



The only thing that jumps at the river is coal burning.

title: Health and Development
text:
First Stage: Air Pollution





TSP concentrations jump by ~200 \(\mu g/m^3\) at the Huai River.

title: Health and Development
text:
The Payoff: Life Expectancy





Life expectancy drops by 5.5 years north of the Huai River.

title: Health and Development
text:
The Numbers


North of the river: TSPs are 184 \(\mu g/m^3\) higher (55% more pollution)
Life expectancy is 5.5 years lower (95% CI: 0.8, 10.2)
Almost entirely due to cardiorespiratory mortality (heart and lung disease)
Noncardiorespiratory mortality: no effect
An additional 100 \(\mu g/m^3\) of TSP → 3.0 fewer years of life expectancy at birth

title: Health and Development
text:
The Scale


The population of Northern China between 1990 and 2000 exceeded 500 million
The Huai River policy led to a staggering loss of over 2.5 billion life years
Current particulate concentrations are 22.9 \(\mu g/m^3\) higher (26% higher north of the river)
Residents of the North continue to have shortened lifespans

title: Health and Development
text:
Complements or Substitutes?


The policy was meant to improve welfare: free heating in cold winters
But it dramatically shortened lives – a negative externality, an unintended consequence
Nobody designed this policy to kill people. But it did.
“These results may help explain why China’s explosive economic growth has led to relatively anemic growth in life expectancy”

title: Health and Development
text:
Using rdrobust

# install.packages("rdrobust")
library(rdrobust)

# Estimate the discontinuity
rd <- rdrobust(y = data$life_expectancy,
               x = data$latitude_from_river,
               c = 0)
summary(rd)



y: outcome variable
x: running variable (distance from cutoff)
c: the cutoff value
rdrobust automatically picks the optimal bandwidth and polynomial

title: Health and Development
text:
Reading the Output


Coefficient: the estimated jump at the cutoff (the treatment effect)
Std. Error: precision of the estimate
p-value: is the jump statistically significant?
Bandwidth: how wide a window around the cutoff is used
N left / N right: how many observations on each side



Same interpretation as lm() — but the estimate is local to the cutoff

title: Health and Development
text:
Simulating an RDD


Show code
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(42)

n <- 200
latitude <- runif(n, -8, 8)
north <- as.numeric(latitude >= 0)

# True effect: 5.5 fewer years north of the river
life_exp <- 78 - 0.3 * latitude - 5.5 * north + rnorm(n, 0, 3)

sim_data <- data.frame(latitude, north, life_exp)

ggplot(sim_data, aes(x = latitude, y = life_exp, color = factor(north))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("0" = "#011F5B", "1" = "red"),
                     labels = c("South", "North")) +
  annotate("label", x = 0, y = 85, label = "Huai River",
           size = 5, color = "grey30") +
  labs(x = "Degrees of latitude from Huai River",
       y = "Life expectancy (years)",
       title = "Simulated RDD: life expectancy drops north of the river",
       color = "") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Health and Development
text:
The Huai River Policy


North: free coal → more coal burning → more air pollution
South: no free coal → less coal burning → less air pollution
This created a massive, arbitrary discontinuity in pollution levels

title: Health and Development
text:
RDD: The Logic


A cutoff assigns treatment: score \(\geq\) 60 → pass
Units just below and just above the cutoff are nearly identical
So any jump in the outcome at the cutoff is the causal effect of treatment
The key assumption: nothing else changes abruptly at the cutoff



This is what Chen et al. exploit: the Huai River is a cutoff that assigns free coal.

title: Health and Development
section: Applying the RDD to the Huai River
text:
Applying the RDD to the Huai River


Running variable: degrees of latitude (distance from the river)
Cutoff: the Huai River (0 degrees)
Treatment: free coal heating (north of the river)
A city 1 degree south vs. 1 degree north: similar climate, similar people, but very different pollution
Compare health outcomes just above and just below the river



Key concern: is there anything else that jumps at the river?

title: Health and Development
section: What Else Could Jump at the River?
text:
What Else Could Jump at the River?


Education, income, urbanization, tap water access: no discontinuity at the river
Temperature and climate: different north vs. south, but change smoothly — no jump
The Huai River cuts through provinces — it is not an administrative boundary
This is always the hardest part of an RDD: you can check observable things, but you can never be 100% sure

text:
The RDD Plot

       x = sim_data$latitude,
       c = 0,
       title = "RDD Plot: Life Expectancy at the Huai River",
       x.label = "Degrees of latitude from Huai River",
       y.label = "Life expectancy (years)")

But China is below the curve — its life expectancy is lower than you would predict from its GDP
Why? Economic growth → pollution, industrial hazards, environmental degradation
Which one dominates depends on policy choices

But development also brings negative externalities:


Air and water pollution

Inequality in who bears the costs

text:
Agenda

The Poverty-Violence Correlation
Two Mechanisms: Opportunity Cost and Rapacity
The Endogeneity Problem
Miguel, Satyanath, and Sergenti (2004)
Instrumental Variables in Practice


Final Project Design due TONIGHT

title: Conflict and Development I
section: Last Week: The State and Security
text:
Last Week: The State and Security

Crime can mobilize citizens (Bateson)
But policing can alienate them (Weaver and Lerman)


Today: Civil war

Civil war as failure of internal security provision
Violence on a scale that reshapes economies and institutions

title: Conflict and Development
text:
The Scale of Civil War


Since 1945, civil wars have killed over 20 million people
Far more than interstate wars in the same period
~20% of the world’s countries experienced civil war in any given year during the Cold War
Concentrated in the poorest countries



Civil war is not just a security problem. It is a development problem.

title: Conflict and Development
text:
A Two-Way Street


Poverty → conflict (grievance, opportunity cost of fighting is low)
Conflict → poverty (destruction, displacement, institutional collapse)
This is the conflict trap (Collier et al., 2003)
Breaking this cycle is one of the hardest challenges in development

title: Conflict and Development
text:
Blattman and Miguel (2010)
A comprehensive review of the causes and consequences of civil war

Today we focus on consequences:


What does civil war destroy?
How long do the effects last?
Can countries recover?

title: Conflict and Development
text:
Human Capital


Death: combat, but mostly civilian casualties from disease, displacement, and famine
Health: malnutrition, disrupted healthcare, psychological trauma
Education: schools destroyed, children recruited into armed groups, families displaced
Akbulut-Yuksel (2014): WWII bombing in Germany reduced schooling by 0.4 years
Akresh and de Walque (2008): Rwandan genocide reduced educational attainment by almost a full year

title: Conflict and Development
text:
Physical Capital


Infrastructure destroyed: roads, bridges, factories, hospitals
Capital flight: investors flee, savings are wiped out
Agricultural collapse: fields mined, livestock killed, markets disrupted
Collier (1999): GDP declines ~2.2% per year during civil war



A 7-year war → economy ~15% smaller than it would have been

title: Conflict and Development
text:
Institutional Collapse


State capacity erodes: tax collection, public services, rule of law
Corruption and war economies: natural resource looting, drug trade
Social trust is damaged
Formal and informal institutions that took decades to build can be destroyed in years

title: Conflict and Development
text:
The Recovery Debate


Pessimistic view: civil war sets countries back decades, effects are permanent
Optimistic view: countries can “bounce back” — the “Phoenix effect”
Miguel and Roland (2011): Vietnam districts that were heavily bombed recovered to similar levels as less-bombed districts
But recovery is uneven: physical capital rebuilds faster than human capital and institutions



The truth is probably somewhere in between — and depends on what was destroyed.

title: Conflict and Development
text:
Context: Northern Uganda


The Lord’s Resistance Army (LRA) waged a brutal insurgency in northern Uganda from the late 1980s
Led by Joseph Kony
The LRA abducted children and young adults to serve as soldiers, porters, and laborers
Tens of thousands abducted, mostly boys aged 10–24

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
The Research Question
Do negative rainfall shocks (droughts) increase the probability of civil conflict?


41 sub-Saharan African countries, 1981-1999
The instrument is rainfall variation: less rain \(\rightarrow\) lower agricultural output \(\rightarrow\) lower economic growth
They use rainfall to isolate the clean part of income variation

title: Conflict and Development
text:
The Identification Problem


You can’t just compare ex-combatants to non-combatants
People who fight may be systematically different: poorer, less educated, more aggressive
Selection bias: the same things that lead to recruitment may also affect outcomes



So how do Blattman and Annan solve this?

title: Conflict and Development
section: The LRA as a Natural Experiment
text:
The LRA as a Natural Experiment


The LRA abducted quasi-randomly: raiding villages, taking whoever was available
Abduction was not based on individual characteristics
Within a given community, who was taken was largely a matter of bad luck — being in the wrong place at the wrong time
This creates something close to random assignment to forced military service



Blattman and Annan verify this: abductees and non-abductees look similar on pre-war characteristics.

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
Data


Countries: 41 sub-Saharan African nations
Period: 1981–1999 (743 country-year observations)
Conflict data: PRIO/Uppsala Armed Conflict Data (≥25 battle deaths per year)
Economic growth: Penn World Tables and World Bank
Rainfall: Global Precipitation Climatology Project (GPCP) — satellite-based, publicly available

title: Conflict and Development
text:
Results: Human Capital


Abductees had 0.75 fewer years of education
Were 10 percentage points less likely to be literate
Large effects on the youngest abductees — those taken during critical schooling years



Abduction interrupted education at a crucial moment, and most never caught up.

title: Conflict and Development
text:
Results: Economic Outcomes


Abductees earned one-third less in daily wages
Were significantly less likely to be engaged in skilled work
More likely to be in subsistence agriculture
The education gap explains much (but not all) of the earnings gap

title: Conflict and Development
text:
Results: Psychological Costs


Abductees reported significantly higher levels of psychological distress
Higher rates of aggression and social difficulties
Those who experienced more violence during captivity had worse outcomes
The psychological scars may be as consequential as the economic ones

title: Conflict and Development
text:
What Do We Learn?


Conflict doesn’t just destroy infrastructure — it destroys people’s potential
Children and young people bear disproportionate costs
The effects persist long after the fighting stops
Education loss alone generates a lifetime of lower earnings
And the psychological costs compound everything

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
Connecting the Pieces


Poverty \(\rightarrow\) conflict is causal (MSS 2004)
But conflict \(\rightarrow\) poverty is also true (next class)
The conflict trap is real and empirically grounded
Breaking it requires addressing both causes and consequences

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
Discussion Questions


If economic shocks cause conflict, what policies could break the cycle?
How do natural resources (oil, diamonds) complicate the picture? Which channel dominates?
Can you think of other instruments for income that might work in different settings?
How does this connect to what we discussed about crime and the state?

title: Conflict and Development I
text: How Common Is Civil War?

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
Civil War by the Numbers


Civil wars have caused three times as many deaths as wars between states since WWII (Fearon and Laitin, 2003)
In sub-Saharan Africa, 27% of country-years experienced civil conflict between 1981 and 1999 (Miguel, Satyanath, and Sergenti, 2004)
Overwhelmingly concentrated in the poorest countries

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
The Conflict Trap
Does poverty actually cause war? Or does civil war cause poverty? Or are they both caused by something else, like geography?

title: Conflict and Development I
text: The Empirical Correlation

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
The Pattern


The poorer the country, the more likely it is to have civil war
This is one of the most robust empirical patterns in the study of conflict
But why?



Two broad families of explanations:


Poverty makes fighting cheaper (opportunity cost)
Poverty makes the state weaker (can’t prevent or deter rebellion)

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
Does Poverty Cause Violence?
Arguments that it does:


Opportunity cost: when you have nothing to lose, fighting is cheap (we’ll formalize this)
State weakness: poor states cannot buy off or suppress rebels
Grievance: deprivation and inequality breed resentment



Arguments that it does not:


Bad institutions may cause both poverty and war
Ethnic fractionalization could drive both
Geography (rough terrain, natural resources) may matter more than income itself

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
What Is Opportunity Cost?
The opportunity cost of doing something is what you give up by doing it



The opportunity cost of joining a rebel group is everything else you could be doing instead
Earning wages, spending time with your family, going to school, farming your land
All of that is increasing in outside wages: the better the economy, the more you give up by fighting

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
Opportunity Cost and Conflict


If wages are $1/day, joining a militia doesn’t cost you much
If wages are $50/day, you are giving up a lot
Poverty lowers the opportunity cost of fighting \(\rightarrow\) more people choose violence



This is the core intuition linking poverty to conflict

title: Conflict and Development I
section: Dal Bo and Dal Bo: Formalizing the Intuition
text:
Dal Bo and Dal Bo: Formalizing the Intuition
A model of conflict between producers and predators:


People choose between two activities: produce (earn wages) or fight (take what others produce)
When wages fall, producing becomes less attractive
Fighting becomes relatively better \(\rightarrow\) more insurrection
This is “insurrection as competition for resources”

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
But Wait: The Rapacity Effect


So far: poverty makes fighting cheaper \(\rightarrow\) more conflict
But what about the opposite?
More resources could mean more things to fight over
Oil is discovered, land becomes more valuable \(\rightarrow\) groups fight harder to capture it
This is the rapacity effect: wealth increases can ALSO cause conflict



So which is it? Does more wealth cause peace or war?

title: Conflict and Development I
section: It Depends on the Type of Economy
text:
It Depends on the Type of Economy


Labor-intensive production (agriculture, manufacturing):

A good economic shock \(\rightarrow\) higher wages \(\rightarrow\) higher opportunity cost of fighting \(\rightarrow\) peace
Example: better harvest \(\rightarrow\) farm workers earn more \(\rightarrow\) less incentive to join a militia

Capital-intensive production (oil, minerals, diamonds):

A good economic shock \(\rightarrow\) more valuable resources to capture \(\rightarrow\) conflict
Example: oil price rises \(\rightarrow\) whoever controls the oil fields gets richer \(\rightarrow\) more worth fighting over




“Whether economic shocks cause peace or war depends on what kind of economy you have”

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
Why This Distinction Matters


Sub-Saharan Africa: economies are overwhelmingly agricultural and labor-intensive
Only 1% of cropland is irrigated in the median African country
Agricultural output depends heavily on rainfall
A drought \(\rightarrow\) lower agricultural income \(\rightarrow\) lower wages \(\rightarrow\) lower opportunity cost of fighting \(\rightarrow\) conflict



This is exactly what Miguel, Satyanath, and Sergenti (2004) will test.

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
Commitment Problems
One more channel linking poverty to conflict:


Even when a bargain exists that both sides prefer to war, groups may not be able to credibly commit to it
If one side could become stronger in the future, the other has incentive to fight now (Fearon, 1995)
Weak states cannot enforce agreements or make credible promises
Weak states tend to be poor states \(\rightarrow\) poverty again

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
War Making as State Making


Tilly (1985): in Europe, war and state-building were intertwined
States that fought wars built fiscal and administrative capacity — taxes, bureaucracies, armies
But in the developing world, colonial borders were imposed — states never went through this process
Many post-colonial states are weak precisely because they were never forged through conflict
This partially explains why civil war concentrates in the Global South

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
Spillovers: War Beyond Borders


Refugee flows destabilize neighboring countries
Arms and combatants cross borders
Regional contagion: conflict in one country increases conflict risk in neighbors
This means conflict is not just a national problem — it is a regional development problem

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
Taking Stock
Multiple channels link poverty to conflict:


Poverty \(\rightarrow\) low opportunity cost \(\rightarrow\) insurrection (Dal Bo and Dal Bo)
Poverty \(\rightarrow\) weak state \(\rightarrow\) commitment problems \(\rightarrow\) conflict
Conflict \(\rightarrow\) destruction \(\rightarrow\) poverty (the trap)



But how do we prove poverty causes conflict? We can’t randomly make countries poor.

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
“Correlation Is Not Causation” (Again)
Blattman and Miguel (2010):

“The correlations of civil conflict with both low income levels and negative income shocks are arguably the most robust empirical patterns in the literature… but the direction of causality remains contested.”



“Even the use of lagged national income growth does not eliminate this concern, since the anticipation of future political instability and conflict can affect current investment behavior and thus living standards.”

title: Conflict and Development I
section: Why Can’t We Just Regress Conflict on Income?
text:
Why Can’t We Just Regress Conflict on Income?
Three problems:


Reverse causality: conflict destroys income — we would confuse the effect with the cause
Omitted variables: bad institutions, ethnic tensions, geography may cause both poverty and conflict
Anticipation: if people expect instability, they stop investing \(\rightarrow\) income falls before conflict starts \(\rightarrow\) even lagged income is contaminated

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
What Would We Need?


Something that changes income but has no direct effect on conflict
Something outside the control of any actor in the conflict
Something that could not be anticipated



We need an exogenous shock to income.


“We can’t randomly assign poverty. But nature randomly assigns droughts.”

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
The State of the World


Sub-Saharan Africa: the region with the most civil wars since 1960
Also the poorest region and the most agriculturally dependent
Agriculture is overwhelmingly rain-fed — only 1% of cropland irrigated
A bad rainfall year means a bad economic year for most African countries

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
The Problem (Again)
We cannot just compare income and conflict:


Richer countries may have better institutions \(\rightarrow\) both higher income AND less conflict
Countries at war have low income because of the war
We need something that shakes income but only income



This is where the instrumental variable comes in.

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
What Is an Instrumental Variable?


Income and conflict are tangled together — we cannot separate cause from effect
We need a third variable — an “instrument” — that:

Affects income (changes how much people earn)
Does NOT directly cause conflict (only matters through income)
Is essentially random (nobody controls it)

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
The Three Conditions
For \(Z\) to be a valid instrument for \(X\) in estimating \(X \rightarrow Y\):


Relevance: \(Z\) actually moves \(X\)

“Does the instrument shift the treatment?”

Exclusion restriction: \(Z\) has no direct arrow to \(Y\)

“The ONLY reason \(Z\) matters for \(Y\) is because it changes \(X\)”

Independence: \(U\) has no arrow to \(Z\)

“Confounders don’t affect the instrument”

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
IV in a Picture
\[\text{Instrument (Z)} \longrightarrow \text{X} \longrightarrow \text{Y}\]
\[\text{Confounders} \longrightarrow \text{X} \text{ AND } \text{Y}\]

\[\text{But: Confounders} \not\longrightarrow \text{Z}\]


Confounders mess up the \(X \rightarrow Y\) relationship — that’s the endogeneity problem
But they do NOT affect \(Z\) — that’s why the instrument works
\(Z\) gives us clean variation in \(X\)

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
How 2SLS Works (Simply)
Two-Stage Least Squares:


Stage 1 (First Stage): Regress income on rainfall

“How much does rainfall predict economic growth?”
If the answer is “a lot,” we have a good instrument

Stage 2 (Second Stage): Regress conflict on predicted income (from Stage 1)

We use only the part of income that was caused by rainfall
This strips out all the confounding — what’s left is the causal effect

title: Conflict and Development I
section: Connecting to Dal Bo and Dal Bo
text:
Connecting to Dal Bo and Dal Bo


Rainfall affects agricultural income — which is labor-intensive
Remember: labor-intensive shocks work through the opportunity cost channel
Rainfall \(\downarrow\) \(\rightarrow\) harvest \(\downarrow\) \(\rightarrow\) wages \(\downarrow\) \(\rightarrow\) opportunity cost of fighting \(\downarrow\) \(\rightarrow\) conflict \(\uparrow\)

title: Conflict and Development I
section: First Stage: Does Rainfall Predict Growth?
text:
First Stage: Does Rainfall Predict Growth?


Current and lagged rainfall growth significantly predict economic growth
A drought leads to roughly a 1-2 percentage point decline in GDP growth

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
First Stage: The Verdict


Current and lagged rainfall growth significantly predict economic growth
A drought year leads to a roughly 1–2 percentage point decline in GDP growth
The relationship is strong — but the F-statistic is 4.5, which is somewhat below the standard threshold of 10
This means we should interpret the IV results with some caution

title: Conflict and Development I
section: Main Results: Does Income Cause Conflict?
text: Main Results: Does Income Cause Conflict?

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
What the Numbers Say


A five-percentage-point decline in economic growth increases the likelihood of civil conflict by roughly 12 percentage points
That is nearly one-half of the average likelihood of conflict in the sample
The effect works through lagged growth — last year’s economic shock predicts this year’s conflict

title: Conflict and Development I
section: OLS vs. IV: A Telling Comparison
text:
OLS vs. IV: A Telling Comparison


The OLS estimates are much smaller and often insignificant
The IV estimates are much larger
Why? The authors argue this reflects measurement error in African income data

OLS with noisy data \(\rightarrow\) attenuation bias (estimates biased toward zero)
IV corrects this by using a cleaner source of variation (rainfall)

Also possible: anticipation bias — people see conflict coming and stop investing, so income falls before the war starts

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
Threats to Inference


Exclusion restriction: could rainfall affect conflict directly?

Harder to fight in mud? Drought causes migration?
Authors argue these are small relative to the economic channel

Weak instrument: F-statistic of 4.5 is below 10

But the reduced form (rainfall \(\rightarrow\) conflict directly) is also significant

External validity: only sub-Saharan Africa, only agrarian economies

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
Implications


Economic shocks cause civil war: the opportunity cost mechanism is supported
Consistent with the labor-intensive channel from Dal Bo and Dal Bo
Policy implication: economic interventions (crop insurance, irrigation, diversification, aid during droughts) could help prevent conflict

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Does War Follow You Home?


Miguel, Saiegh, and Satyanath (2011) study thousands of professional soccer players in European leagues
They compare players from countries with civil war histories to players from peaceful countries
Players from civil war countries receive significantly more yellow and red cards — even controlling for position, age, league, and talent
But they do NOT score more or fewer goals — the effect is specific to violent behavior



Conflict doesn’t just destroy economies. It changes people.

title: Conflict and Development II
text: The Soccer Data

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Why This Matters


Violence “follows people” even outside the conflict zone
The consequences of war extend beyond economics — they are behavioral and psychological
This motivates our question today: what does conflict destroy, and how long do the effects last?

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Last Class


Poverty lowers the opportunity cost of fighting (Dal Bo and Dal Bo)
Weak states cannot credibly commit to peace
Miguel, Satyanath, and Sergenti (2004): rainfall shocks \(\rightarrow\) income drops \(\rightarrow\) civil conflict
The causal link from poverty to conflict is real



Today: the other side of the conflict trap. What does conflict cause?

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Blattman and Miguel (2010)
A comprehensive review of the causes and consequences of civil war

Three categories of destruction:


Human capital: lives, health, education
Physical capital: infrastructure, assets, investment
Institutions: state capacity, trust, rule of law

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Human Capital


War-related malnutrition in Zimbabwe: children ended up significantly shorter as adults (Alderman, Hoddinott, and Kinsey, 2006)
Rwandan genocide reduced educational attainment by almost a full year (Akresh and de Walque, 2008)
In Burundi, children in war-affected regions had height-for-age ~0.5 standard deviations lower (Bundervoet, Verwimp, and Akresh, 2009)

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Physical Capital


Infrastructure destroyed: roads, bridges, factories, hospitals
Capital flight: mobile capital flees to foreign assets; new investment dries up
Agricultural collapse: in Mozambique, 80% of the cattle stock was lost; in northern Uganda, families lost cattle, homes, and assets (Blattman and Miguel, 2010)
Cerra and Saxena (2008): output declines 6% in the immediate aftermath of civil war



But physical capital can recover — cities bombed in WWII (Japan, Germany) returned to pre-war population trends within 20–25 years.

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Institutional Collapse


State capacity erodes: tax collection, public services, rule of law
Corruption and war economies emerge: natural resource looting, drug trade
Social trust is damaged
Formal and informal institutions that took decades to build can be destroyed in years



Blattman and Miguel (2010): “The social and institutional legacies of conflict are arguably the most important but least understood of all war impacts”

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
The Recovery Debate


Pessimistic view: civil war sets countries back decades, effects are permanent
Optimistic view: countries can “bounce back” — the “Phoenix effect”
Miguel and Roland (2011): Vietnam districts that were heavily bombed recovered to similar economic levels as less-bombed districts
But recovery is uneven: physical capital rebuilds faster than human capital and institutions



The truth depends on what was destroyed — and on who was affected.

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Context: Northern Uganda


The Lord’s Resistance Army (LRA) waged a brutal insurgency in northern Uganda from the late 1980s
Led by Joseph Kony
The LRA abducted children and young adults to serve as soldiers, porters, and laborers
Tens of thousands abducted, mostly boys aged 10-24

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
The Research Question
What are the long-run consequences of forced military service on:


Human capital (education, skills)
Economic outcomes (employment, earnings)
Psychological well-being



Why is this hard to study?

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
The Identification Problem


You can’t just compare ex-combatants to non-combatants
People who fight may be systematically different: poorer, less educated, more aggressive
Selection bias: the same things that lead to recruitment may also affect outcomes

title: Conflict and Development II
section: The LRA as a Natural Experiment
text:
The LRA as a Natural Experiment
The LRA’s abduction strategy was essentially random:


“Targets were generally unplanned and arbitrary; they raided whatever homesteads they encountered” (p. 887)
Strategy: abduct first, sort out later: keep all adolescent and young adult males
Rural Acholi households live in isolation, making them vulnerable to roving raiding parties
Within a community, who was taken was largely a matter of bad luck

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Data


Survey of 741 male youth aged 14-30 in 2005-2006
8 sub-counties in two war-affected districts (Kitgum and Pader)
Compared abductees to non-abductees within the same communities
Outcomes: years of education, literacy, daily earnings, employment type, psychological distress

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Results: Human Capital


Abductees had 0.75 fewer years of education: a 10% reduction
Were 15 percentage points less likely to be functionally literate
Largest effects on the youngest abductees: those taken during critical schooling years



Why would age at abduction matter?

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Results: Economic Outcomes


Abductees’ wages were 33% lower
Significantly less likely to be engaged in skilled work
More likely to be in subsistence agriculture
The education gap explains much (but not all) of the earnings gap



If education doesn’t explain the full gap, what else could?

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Results: Psychological Costs


Abductees reported significantly higher levels of psychological distress
Higher rates of aggression and social difficulties
The intensity of violence experienced matters more than the duration of abduction
Someone abducted for 6 months who saw killings had worse outcomes than someone abducted for 2 years who did not

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
What Do We Learn?


Conflict doesn’t just destroy infrastructure: it destroys people’s potential
Children and young people are both the victims and the fighters: they lose schooling years they cannot recover, and they carry the trauma of combat
The effects persist long after the fighting stops
Education loss generates a lifetime of lower earnings; psychological distress makes reintegration harder

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
The Conflict Trap, Revisited


Last class: poverty causes conflict (MSS 2004)
Today: conflict destroys human capital, physical capital, institutions, and people’s psychology
Destroyed human capital \(\rightarrow\) lower earnings \(\rightarrow\) poverty \(\rightarrow\) more conflict
The micro evidence (Blattman and Annan) confirms the macro pattern (Blattman and Miguel review)



The trap is real. How do you break it?

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Discussion Questions


Given what MSS showed about economic shocks causing conflict, and what we see here about conflict destroying human capital — how does the trap perpetuate itself?
What kinds of post-conflict interventions would address the damage documented by Blattman and Annan?
Is physical capital or human capital harder to rebuild? Why?
The soccer paper shows behavioral effects far from the conflict zone. What does this imply for refugee and diaspora communities?

From destruction to movement: what happens when people leave?

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
Where We Focus Today
We will develop two mechanisms in detail:


Opportunity cost: poverty makes fighting cheap (Dal Bo and Dal Bo)
Rapacity: wealth can also cause conflict — it depends on the type of economy



Then: commitment problems as an additional channel, and the endogeneity problem that makes all of this hard to prove.

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
The Rapacity Effect


So far: poverty makes fighting cheaper. Fewer resources \(\rightarrow\) more conflict
But what about the opposite?
More resources could mean more things to fight over
Oil is discovered, land becomes more valuable \(\rightarrow\) groups fight harder to capture it
This is the rapacity effect: wealth increases can ALSO cause conflict



So which is it? Does more wealth cause peace or war?

title: Conflict and Development I
section: The Economic Makeup of a Country Shapes the Answer
text:
The Economic Makeup of a Country Shapes the Answer


Labor-intensive production (agriculture, manufacturing):

A good economic shock \(\rightarrow\) higher wages \(\rightarrow\) higher opportunity cost of fighting \(\rightarrow\) peace
Example: better harvest \(\rightarrow\) farm workers earn more \(\rightarrow\) less incentive to join a militia

Capital-intensive production (oil, minerals, diamonds):

A good economic shock \(\rightarrow\) more valuable resources to capture \(\rightarrow\) conflict
Example: oil price rises \(\rightarrow\) whoever controls the oil fields gets richer \(\rightarrow\) more worth fighting over

title: Conflict and Development I
section: Because Economic Makeup Covaries with Violence
text:
Because Economic Makeup Covaries with Violence


Sub-Saharan Africa: overwhelmingly agricultural and labor-intensive
Only ~1% of cropland is irrigated in the median African country
Agricultural output depends heavily on rainfall
A drought \(\rightarrow\) lower agricultural income \(\rightarrow\) lower wages \(\rightarrow\) lower opportunity cost of fighting \(\rightarrow\) conflict



This is exactly what Miguel, Satyanath, and Sergenti (2004) will test.

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
War Making and State Making


Tilly (1985): in Europe, war and state-building were intertwined
States that fought wars built fiscal and administrative capacity
In the developing world, colonial borders were imposed — states never went through this process
Many post-colonial states are weak precisely because they were never forged through conflict

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
Correlation Is Not Causation
Blattman and Miguel (2010):

“The correlations of civil conflict with both low income levels and negative income shocks are arguably the most robust empirical patterns in the literature… but the direction of causality remains contested.”



“Even the use of lagged national income growth does not eliminate this concern, since the anticipation of future political instability and conflict can affect current investment behavior and thus living standards.”

title: Conflict and Development I
section: Three Problems with a Naive Regression
text:
Three Problems with a Naive Regression


Reverse causality: conflict destroys income, so we confuse the effect with the cause
Omitted variables: institutions, ethnic tensions, geography may cause both poverty and conflict
Anticipation: if people expect instability, they stop investing \(\rightarrow\) income falls before conflict starts



We need something that changes income but has no direct effect on conflict

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
The Setting


Sub-Saharan Africa: the region with the most civil wars since 1960
Also the poorest and most agriculturally dependent region
Agriculture is overwhelmingly rain-fed: only ~1% of cropland irrigated
When rainfall drops, harvests fail, and the economy contracts

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
How 2SLS Works
Two-Stage Least Squares:


Stage 1: Regress \(X\) on \(Z\)

This gives us \(\widehat{X}\): the part of \(X\) that is explained by \(Z\)
\(\widehat{X}\) contains only clean variation; the dirty part is left in the residuals

Stage 2: Regress \(Y\) on \(\widehat{X}\)

We threw away the contaminated variation and kept only the clean part
What’s left is the causal effect of \(X\) on \(Y\)

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
First Stage Results


Current and lagged rainfall growth significantly predict economic growth
A drought year leads to roughly 1–2 percentage point decline in GDP growth
F-statistic is 4.5, below the standard threshold of 10
Results should be interpreted with some caution

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
OLS vs. IV


OLS estimates are much smaller and often insignificant
IV estimates are larger — why?
Measurement error in African income data \(\rightarrow\) attenuation bias in OLS
Anticipation bias — investment falls before war starts, contaminating OLS
IV isolates the part of income variation driven by rainfall — cleaner signal

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
Arguments That Poverty Causes Violence


Opportunity cost: when you have nothing to lose, fighting is cheap
State weakness: poor states cannot buy off or suppress rebels
Grievance: deprivation and inequality breed resentment

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
Arguments That It Does Not


Bad institutions may cause both poverty and war
Geography could cause both
The causation could go in the other direction: conflict causes poverty



Today we focus on two mechanisms that formalize the “yes” side

title: Conflict and Development I
section: Dal Bo and Dal Bo: A Model
text:
Dal Bo and Dal Bo: A Model
A formal model of conflict between producers and predators:


People choose between two activities: produce (earn wages) or fight (take what others produce)
When wages fall, producing becomes less attractive
Fighting becomes relatively better \(\rightarrow\) more insurrection

title: Conflict and Development I
section: It Depends: Can You Pillage It?
text:
It Depends: Can You Pillage It?


Labor-intensive wealth (agriculture, manufacturing):

You can’t steal someone’s harvest without a workforce: the value is in the labor
A good economic shock to labor intensive products \(\rightarrow\) higher wages \(\rightarrow\) higher opportunity cost \(\rightarrow\) peace

Capital-intensive wealth (oil, minerals, diamonds):

You CAN seize a mine or an oil field: the value is in the ground
A good economic shock to capital intensive products \(\rightarrow\) more valuable prize to capture \(\rightarrow\) conflict

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
The Takeaway


Poverty \(\rightarrow\) low opportunity cost \(\rightarrow\) insurrection (opportunity cost channel)
Wealth \(\rightarrow\) more to fight over \(\rightarrow\) conflict (rapacity channel)
Which one dominates depends on the economic structure of the country



But how do we prove any of this? We can’t randomly make countries poor.

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
The Key Results


First stage: rainfall strongly predicts economic growth in rain-fed agricultural economies
Second stage: a 5 percentage-point decline in economic growth increases the likelihood of civil conflict by roughly 12 percentage points
That is nearly one-half of the average likelihood of conflict in the sample
The effect works through lagged growth — last year’s drought predicts this year’s conflict

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
Connecting Back to Theory


Rainfall affects agricultural income: labor-intensive
You can’t pillage labor so this is a shock to the opportunity cost channel
Drought \(\rightarrow\) harvest falls \(\rightarrow\) wages fall \(\rightarrow\) opportunity cost of fighting falls \(\rightarrow\) conflict rises
MSS provides evidence for the Dal Bo and Dal Bo mechanism

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
IV in R

library(ivreg)

# OLS: uses all variation in growth (clean + dirty)
ols <- lm(conflict ~ growth, data = mss)

# IV: uses only the part of growth driven by rainfall
iv <- ivreg(conflict ~ growth | rainfall, data = mss)

summary(iv, diagnostics = TRUE)
