section: What the IV Output Tells You
text:
What the IV Output Tells You

# Key things to check:
# 1. First-stage F-statistic — is the instrument strong?
#    Rule of thumb: F > 10 (MSS gets 4.5, borderline)

# 2. Coefficients — the causal effect of growth on conflict
#    MSS: 5pp decline in growth → ~12pp increase in conflict

# 3. Compare to OLS — if IV > OLS, likely measurement error
#    or anticipation bias in OLS

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
When Is IV Useful?


When you suspect endogeneity: reverse causality, omitted variables, anticipation
When you can find a variable that is:

Relevant (actually moves \(X\))
Excludable (only affects \(Y\) through \(X\))
Independent (not driven by confounders)

The hardest part is always the exclusion restriction: you can’t test it, you have to argue it

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
Is the Relationship Causal?
Does poverty actually cause war?

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
The Theoretical Takeaway


Poverty \(\rightarrow\) low opportunity cost \(\rightarrow\) insurrection (opportunity cost channel)
Wealth \(\rightarrow\) more to fight over \(\rightarrow\) conflict (rapacity channel)
Which one dominates depends on the economic structure of the country



But how do we prove any of this? We can’t randomly make countries poor

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
The Main Results


First stage: rainfall strongly predicts economic growth in rain-fed agricultural economies
Second stage: a 5 percentage-point decline in economic growth increases the likelihood of civil conflict by roughly 12 percentage points
That is nearly one-half of the average likelihood of conflict in the sample
The effect works through lagged growth — last year’s drought predicts this year’s conflict

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
The Idea
Imagine you want to know if \(X\) causes \(Y\), but they are tangled together:


\(X\) might cause \(Y\)
But \(Y\) might also cause \(X\)
And some third thing might cause both



You need a backdoor — a variable that nudges \(X\) but has nothing to do with \(Y\) except through \(X\).

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
An Everyday Analogy
Does drinking coffee make you more productive?


Problem: maybe productive people just drink more coffee
What if your commute route determines whether you pass a coffee shop?
Your commute route affects your coffee intake…
…but has no direct effect on your productivity
So any change in productivity linked to commute-driven coffee is causal



The commute route is the instrument.

title: Conflict and Development I
section: Why Rainfall Works as an Instrument
text:
Why Rainfall Works as an Instrument


Relevance: droughts destroy harvests \(\rightarrow\) lower income
Exclusion: rainfall affects conflict only because it changes income
Independence: nobody controls the weather


\[\text{Rainfall} \longrightarrow \text{Economic Growth} \longrightarrow \text{Conflict}\]

title: Conflict and Development I
section: Second Stage: Does Income Cause Conflict?
text:
Second Stage: Does Income Cause Conflict?


A 5 percentage-point decline in economic growth increases the likelihood of civil conflict by roughly 12 percentage points
That is nearly one-half of the average likelihood of conflict in the sample
The effect works through lagged growth — last year’s drought predicts this year’s conflict

title: Conflict and Development I
section: OLS vs. IV: Why Does It Matter?
text:
OLS vs. IV: Why Does It Matter?


OLS estimates are much smaller and often insignificant
IV estimates are larger — why?
Measurement error in African income data \(\rightarrow\) attenuation bias in OLS
Anticipation bias — investment falls before war starts, contaminating OLS
IV isolates the part of income variation driven by rainfall — cleaner signal

title: Conflict and Development I
section: What to Look For in IV Output
text:
What to Look For in IV Output

# 1. First-stage F-statistic
#    Is the instrument strong? Rule of thumb: F > 10
#    MSS gets 4.5 — borderline weak

# 2. IV coefficients vs. OLS coefficients
#    If IV > OLS: measurement error or anticipation bias
#    If IV < OLS: OLS was picking up reverse causality

# 3. The exclusion restriction
#    You CANNOT test this statistically
#    You have to argue it. This is always the hard part.

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
The Core Intuition
Think of \(X\) (income) as having two parts:


Clean variation: changes in income driven by forces that have nothing to do with conflict
Dirty variation: changes in income tangled up with confounders, reverse causality, anticipation



OLS uses all the variation in \(X\): clean and dirty mixed together


An instrument \(Z\) lets us extract only the clean part. If \(Z\) moves \(X\) but has absolutely no relationship with \(Y\) except through \(X\), then the piece of \(X\) that \(Z\) explains is pure signal

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
An Analogy
You want to know if class size (\(X\)) affects test scores (\(Y\)).


Problem: rich districts have small classes AND high scores. Is it the class size or the wealth?
Now imagine some districts get randomly assigned extra funding (\(Z\)) through a lottery
Lottery winners hire more teachers \(\rightarrow\) smaller classes
The lottery has no direct effect on test scores — it only matters because it changes class size
So: compare scores in lottery-winner districts vs. losers \(\rightarrow\) causal effect of class size



The lottery is the instrument. It gives us clean variation in class size.

title: Conflict and Development I
text: IV as a DAG

title: Conflict and Development I
section: When Does the Exclusion Restriction Fail?
text:
When Does the Exclusion Restriction Fail?
The exclusion restriction says: \(Z\) affects \(Y\) only through \(X\). No other path.

It would fail if \(Z\) affects something else that also affects \(Y\):


Example: rain \(\rightarrow\) roads wash out \(\rightarrow\) harder to move troops \(\rightarrow\) conflict changes (not through income!)
Example: rain \(\rightarrow\) disease outbreaks \(\rightarrow\) population displacement \(\rightarrow\) conflict changes
Example: rain \(\rightarrow\) crop failure \(\rightarrow\) migration \(\rightarrow\) conflict in neighboring regions




You cannot test this statistically. You have to argue it. This is always the hardest part of IV.

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
An Example
Does education (\(X\)) increase earnings (\(Y\))?


Dirty variation: motivated people get more education AND earn more: is it the schooling or the motivation?
Observation: people who grew up closer to a college tend to get more education (Card, 1993)
Proximity to a college (\(Z\)) shifts education for geographic reasons, not because of ability or motivation
The part of education explained by distance is clean: free of the motivation confound
Use only that clean part \(\rightarrow\) causal effect of education on earnings

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
Second Stage: The Causal Effect
The decline in economic growth caused by drought increases conflict:


A 5 percentage-point decline in rainfall-driven growth increases the likelihood of civil conflict by roughly 12 percentage points
The effect comes through lagged growth: last year’s drought predicts this year’s conflict

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
Does the Exclusion Restriction Hold?
The instrument is only valid if rainfall affects conflict exclusively through income. But what if:


Drought \(\rightarrow\) roads deteriorate \(\rightarrow\) harder to move troops \(\rightarrow\) conflict changes for logistical reasons, not income
Drought \(\rightarrow\) disease outbreaks \(\rightarrow\) displacement \(\rightarrow\) conflict over new territory
Drought \(\rightarrow\) crop failure \(\rightarrow\) migration to neighboring regions \(\rightarrow\) conflict there



The authors argue these channels are small relative to the economic channel. You cannot test this statistically: you have to argue it

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
Weak Instrument?


F-statistic of 4.5 is below the conventional threshold of 10
This means the instrument may not be strong enough to fully trust the IV estimates
However, the reduced form (rainfall \(\rightarrow\) conflict directly, skipping the two stages) is also significant
External validity is limited: only sub-Saharan Africa, only agrarian economies

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
The Poverty Trap
We now have evidence running in both directions:


Poverty \(\rightarrow\) conflict (MSS: economic shocks cause civil war)
Conflict \(\rightarrow\) poverty (next class: war destroys human capital, infrastructure, institutions)
Countries can get stuck: poverty breeds conflict, conflict deepens poverty



How do you break the cycle? How do countries move from vicious spirals to virtuous ones?

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
Discussion


MSS show that droughts cause conflict in agrarian economies. What would you expect in oil-rich countries: more conflict or less?
Bateson argued crime can push citizens toward political participation. Could the same logic apply to civil war?
We’ve now seen the state fail at two scales: policing and civil war. What makes some weak states experience crime while others tip into full-scale war?

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
What Is a Civil War?
What makes something a “civil war”?

Every definition is contested. One that is widely used is the Uppsala/PRIO definition:

“A contested incompatibility which concerns government and/or territory where the use of armed force between two parties, of which at least one is the government of a state, results in at least 25 battle-related deaths”



Note what this excludes: one-sided violence against civilians, non-state conflict between militias, anything below 25 deaths

title: Conflict and Development I
text:
From Crime to Civil War
Last class we talked about crime and the state:


Crime emerges when the state fails to provide internal security
Civil war: some people actively fight the state



Is there a continuum from crime to organized violence to civil war? Or are these fundamentally different phenomena?

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
What Causes Conflict?


Poverty lowers the opportunity cost of fighting (Dal Bo and Dal Bo)
Wealth can also cause conflict if it increases the returns to fighting: rapacity
Other explanations: grievance, ethnic fractionalization, weak institutions
Conflict is both a cause and a consequence of poverty complicating causal analyses
We used instrumental variables to try to isolate the causal effect of income on conflict



Today: the other side. What does conflict do to people?

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
A Surprising Finding
Blattman (2009), using the same natural experiment in northern Uganda, finds:


Abductees were more likely to vote than non-abductees
More likely to be community leaders
More engaged in collective action



This is counterintuitive: violence seems to increase political participation, not decrease it

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Connecting to Bateson
Remember Bateson (2012) from the crime class:


Crime victims in Latin America were more likely to participate in politics
Victimization can be a mobilizing experience: people who have been harmed demand change
Blattman finds the same pattern with war: exposure to violence pushes people toward political engagement



Violence destroys human capital and economic prospects, but it can also politicize people

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
The Paradox of Conflict’s Consequences


Destructive: less education, lower earnings, psychological trauma (Blattman and Annan)
Mobilizing: more political participation, more collective action (Blattman 2009, Bateson 2012)
These are not contradictory: people who have suffered may have both worse economic outcomes AND stronger motivation to engage politically



The consequences of conflict are not one-dimensional

title: Conflict and Development II
section: Civil War Exposure and Violence on the Soccer Pitch
text:
Civil War Exposure and Violence on the Soccer Pitch


Study thousands of professional soccer players in European leagues
Compare players from countries with civil war histories to players from peaceful countries
Players from civil war countries receive significantly more yellow and red cards
But they do NOT score more or fewer goals: the effect is specific to violent behavior

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Why Soccer?


Soccer provides a controlled setting: same rules, same refs, same competition
Players from different countries face each other on a level playing field
Violent behavior (fouls, cards) is clearly measured and recorded
Allows separation of aggression from skill

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
What This Tells Us


Violence “follows people” even outside the conflict zone
The consequences of war extend beyond economics: they are behavioral
Civil war exposure during childhood shapes how people interact with others years later
Connects to Blattman and Annan’s finding on psychological distress and aggression

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Putting It Together


Last class: poverty causes conflict (MSS)
Today: conflict destroys human capital and earnings (Blattman and Annan)
Destroyed human capital \(\rightarrow\) lower earnings \(\rightarrow\) poverty \(\rightarrow\) more conflict
But conflict also politicizes people (Blattman, Bateson)
And changes behavior long after the war ends (Miguel, Saiegh, Satyanath)

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Discussion


Blattman and Annan show economic devastation; Blattman (2009) shows political mobilization. Can both be true? What does that mean for post-conflict societies?
The soccer paper shows behavioral effects far from the conflict zone. What does this imply for refugee and diaspora communities?
If the consequences of conflict are this persistent, what kinds of interventions could actually help?

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Physical Capital and Institutions


In Mozambique, 80% of the cattle stock was lost during the civil war
Cerra and Saxena (2008): output declines 6% in the immediate aftermath of civil war
State capacity erodes: tax collection, public services, rule of law
Social trust is damaged; corruption and war economies emerge



But some places recover: cities bombed in WWII returned to pre-war population trends within 20-25 years. What determines whether destruction is permanent?

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Beyond Economics


Conflict doesn’t just destroy infrastructure and income
It changes people: their health, their psychology, their behavior
How do we measure these less visible consequences?



This is where Blattman and Annan come in

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Three Kinds of Destruction


Physical capital: roads, bridges, factories, livestock
Human capital: education interrupted, health damaged, skills lost
People themselves: psychology, behavior, trust



Most of what we know about the first two comes from macro data. To understand the third, we need micro evidence: what happens to individuals?

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
What Should We Expect?
Two hypotheses about what forced military service does to young people:


H1 (human capital): abduction interrupts education and skill formation \(\rightarrow\) lower earnings, worse economic outcomes
H2 (psychology): exposure to extreme violence \(\rightarrow\) lasting psychological distress, aggression, difficulty reintegrating



What does the evidence say?

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Data and Design


Survey of 741 male youth aged 14-30 in 2005-2006
From 8 sub-counties in two war-affected districts (Kitgum and Pader)
Compared abductees to non-abductees within the same communities
Key: because abduction was quasi-random, this is close to comparing treatment and control groups in an experiment

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
The Mechanism


Is it just lost schooling? Or something deeper?
Blattman and Annan decompose the earnings gap:

Education accounts for a large share
But psychological distress independently predicts worse outcomes
Those who witnessed or committed more violence during captivity had worse outcomes even conditional on education

Violence itself leaves a mark, beyond the years of school missed

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Violence and Political Participation
In a companion paper, Blattman (2009) uses the same natural experiment in northern Uganda and finds something unexpected:


Abductees were more likely to vote than non-abductees
More likely to be community leaders
More engaged in collective action



Development outcomes worsen, but political participation increases

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Why?


Exposure to violence may change people’s relationship to the state: they want to shape the political order that failed to protect them
War creates shared identity among survivors and a sense of collective purpose
Similar to what Bateson (2012) found with crime: victimization can be a mobilizing experience



How can the same experience destroy someone’s economic prospects and make them MORE politically engaged? What does that tell us about what conflict does to people?

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
The Hypothesis
If civil war shapes behavior, can we detect it outside the conflict zone?


Professional soccer players come from all over the world and compete in European leagues
They play under identical rules, with the same referees, in the same competitions
Violent behavior on the pitch (fouls, yellow and red cards) is recorded precisely
Hypothesis: players from countries with civil war histories will exhibit more violent behavior on the field

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
The Data


Thousands of players in top European leagues (England, France, Germany, Italy, Spain)
Outcome variables: yellow cards, red cards, goals scored
Treatment: years of civil war in the player’s home country (1980-2005)
Player-level data on position, age, minutes played, league, team

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Results





Yellow cards and civil war exposure (conditional on controls)

title: Conflict and Development II
text: The Regression Table

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
What the Results Show


More years of civil war in a player’s home country \(\rightarrow\) significantly more yellow and red cards
But civil war exposure has no effect on goals scored: the effect is specific to aggression, not skill
The result holds controlling for player position, age, league, and team quality
Robust to dropping outliers (Colombia, Israel)

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Connecting the Papers


Blattman and Annan: conflict destroys education, earnings, psychological health
Blattman (2009): but it also increases political engagement
Miguel, Saiegh, Satyanath: and it changes behavior years later, thousands of miles away
The common thread: war reshapes the people who lived through it

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Motivation
Blattman and Annan showed conflict changes people psychologically: more distress, more aggression

But that evidence comes from within the conflict zone


Can we detect behavioral consequences of war in a completely different setting, years later, thousands of miles away?

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
The Setting: European Soccer


Professional soccer is one of the few places where people from very different countries compete in a controlled environment
Same rules, same referees, same leagues
Violent behavior (fouls, yellow and red cards) is precisely recorded
Skill (goals, assists) is also recorded



This gives us a natural way to separate aggression from ability

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Research Question
What are the long-run consequences of forced military service on education, economic outcomes, and psychological well-being?

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
The Hypothesis and Mechanism


Hypothesis: civil war exposure during formative years increases propensity toward violent behavior, even in non-war settings
Mechanism: growing up in a violent environment normalizes aggression as a response to conflict and competition
Alternative: maybe war countries produce players from poorer backgrounds who play more aggressively out of desperation, not socialization

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Identification Strategy


Compare players from different countries playing in the same league
Controls: player position, age, minutes played, team quality, league
The key variation: two players on the same team, same position, same age, but one is from a country with 10 years of civil war and the other from a peaceful country
Assumption: conditional on controls, a player’s nationality is not correlated with unobserved determinants of on-field aggression

title: Conflict and Development II
text: Descriptive Evidence

title: Conflict and Development II
text: Main Results

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Interpreting the Results


More years of civil war in a player’s home country \(\rightarrow\) significantly more yellow and red cards
Civil war exposure has no effect on goals scored: the effect is specific to aggression, not skill or effort
Result holds controlling for player position, age, league, and team quality
Robust to dropping outliers (Colombia, Israel)

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Threats and Limitations


Selection: maybe only the most aggressive players from war countries make it to European leagues?
Referee bias: could referees card players from certain countries more harshly?
Omitted variables: poverty, inequality, and culture may correlate with both war and aggression
The authors address some of these but none can be fully ruled out

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Threats


Selection: maybe only the most aggressive players from war countries make it to European leagues
Referee bias: could referees card players from certain countries more harshly?
Omitted variables: poverty, inequality, culture may correlate with both war and aggression



How would you design a test to rule out referee bias? Hint: think about what should vary if it’s the ref’s perception vs the player’s behavior

title: Conflict and Development II
section: Placebo Tests: What Else Should Be True?
text:
Placebo Tests: What Else Should Be True?
If the hypothesis is correct (war exposure \(\rightarrow\) aggression), certain things should and should NOT hold:


Should be true: the effect should be stronger for players who were younger during the civil war (more impressionable)
Should be true: the effect should be specific to violent behavior (cards), not skill (goals)
Should NOT be true: civil war exposure should NOT predict goals scored. If it did, that would suggest something else is going on (e.g. desperation, playing style)



This is the logic of a placebo test in observational data: if your story is right, it should predict some outcomes and NOT others. The “no effect on goals” result is a placebo: it rules out alternative explanations where war exposure just makes you a different kind of player

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Placebo Tests in Observational Data
How do you build confidence in a result you can’t experimentally verify?


Ask: if my story is right, what else should be true?
And critically: what should NOT be true?
If your treatment affects an outcome it shouldn’t, your story has a problem
If it does NOT affect that outcome, that’s reassuring



A placebo test checks whether the pattern is specific to the mechanism you claim

title: Conflict and Development II
section: Placebo Tests in the Soccer Paper
text:
Placebo Tests in the Soccer Paper


Should be true: civil war exposure \(\rightarrow\) more yellow and red cards (aggression) \(\checkmark\)
Should NOT be true: civil war exposure \(\rightarrow\) more goals scored

If war exposure predicted goals, that would suggest it’s capturing playing style or desperation, not aggression specifically
Result: no effect on goals \(\checkmark\)

Should be true: effect stronger for players who were younger during the civil war (more impressionable during formative years)



The “no effect on goals” result is the placebo: it rules out stories where war just makes you a different kind of player

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Setting


Northern Uganda, late 1980s onwards
The Lord’s Resistance Army (LRA), led by Joseph Kony, waged a brutal insurgency
The LRA abducted children and young adults to serve as soldiers, porters, and laborers
Tens of thousands abducted, mostly boys aged 10-24



What do you think happens to these children in the long run?

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Hypothesis
H1: civil war exposure during formative years increases propensity toward violent behavior, even outside of war

Mechanism: growing up surrounded by violence normalizes aggression as a way of dealing with conflict and competition


What alternative stories could explain the same pattern?

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Strategy
The LRA’s abduction strategy was essentially random:


“Targets were generally unplanned and arbitrary; they raided whatever homesteads they encountered” (p. 887)
Strategy: abduct first, sort out later: keep all adolescent and young adult males
Rural Acholi households live in isolation, making them vulnerable to roving raiding parties
Within a community, who was taken was largely a matter of bad luck



What assumption does this rely on? What could go wrong?

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Reading the Table


More years of civil war \(\rightarrow\) significantly more yellow and red cards
No effect on goals scored: aggression, not skill
Holds controlling for position, age, league, team quality
Robust to dropping outliers (Colombia, Israel)



Why does the “no effect on goals” matter?

title: Conflict and Development II
text:
Placebo Tests in This Paper


Should be true: civil war exposure \(\rightarrow\) more cards (aggression) \(\checkmark\)
Should NOT be true: civil war exposure \(\rightarrow\) more goals

If war predicted goals, something else is going on: playing style, desperation, not aggression
Result: no effect on goals \(\checkmark\)

Should be true: effect stronger for players younger during the civil war (more impressionable)



The “no effect on goals” is the placebo: it rules out stories where war just makes you a different kind of player

H1 (human capital): abduction interrupts education and skill formation \(\rightarrow\) lower earnings, worse economic outcomes
H2 (psychology): exposure to extreme violence \(\rightarrow\) lasting psychological distress, aggression, difficulty reintegrating



What would make this hard to study? Why can’t we just compare soldiers to non-soldiers?

Mechanism: Decomposing the Earnings Gap


Education accounts for a large share of the earnings difference
But psychological distress independently predicts worse outcomes, even conditional on education
Those who witnessed or committed more violence during captivity had worse outcomes regardless of schooling
It’s not just lost years of school: violence itself leaves a mark

title: Migration and Development
section: Last Class: The Consequences of Civil War
text:
Last Class: The Consequences of Civil War


Conflict destroys human capital, changes behavior, politicizes people
One of the most immediate consequences of conflict is displacement
Today: what does migration mean for development?

title: Migration and Development
text:
The Decision to Migrate


Frame it in terms of opportunity cost: what are the returns of being somewhere else vs staying?
Moving from a poor to a rich country can 2-3x your earnings overnight
Migration may be the single most effective way to increase someone’s income
Like conflict, the decision to migrate depends on expected returns relative to the status quo

title: Migration and Development
text:
Types of Migration


Forced: conflict, persecution, disaster (refugees, asylum seekers, IDPs)
Voluntary: economic opportunity, family reunification, education
The line between the two is often blurry: conflict destroys livelihoods, poverty makes people vulnerable to violence

title: Migration and Development
text: The Scale

title: Migration and Development
text:
The Counterintuitive Finding


It is NOT the poorest who migrate
Migration requires resources: savings for travel, networks at the destination, information about opportunities
The people trapped in the worst poverty often can’t move
Migration is a development tool that doesn’t reach the people who need it most



What does this imply for migration as anti-poverty policy?

title: Migration and Development
text:
Selection


Migrants are not a random sample of the origin population
They tend to be younger, healthier, more educated, more risk-tolerant
This creates a measurement problem: if we compare migrants to non-migrants, we’re comparing different kinds of people
Sound familiar? (Connect to selection bias in Blattman and Annan)

title: Migration and Development
text:
Setting


The Philippines: one of the world’s largest migrant-sending countries
Millions of Filipino workers abroad, mostly in the Middle East, East Asia, and the US
They send remittances home to their families
What do families do with this money?

title: Migration and Development
text:
Research Question
Do remittances increase household investment in human capital and entrepreneurship in origin communities?

What would you predict? Do families spend remittances on consumption (food, goods) or investment (education, business)?

title: Migration and Development
text:
Hypothesis


H1: remittance income increases investment in education and entrepreneurship
Mechanism: remittances relax credit constraints that prevent poor households from making productive investments
Alternative: families might just consume more (better food, nicer house) without changing their long-run trajectory

title: Migration and Development
text:
The Identification Problem


Can’t just compare households that receive remittances to those that don’t
Households with migrants abroad are different: more connected, more entrepreneurial, possibly wealthier to begin with
Need exogenous variation in remittance income



What could serve as an instrument here?

title: Migration and Development
text:
Strategy


Filipino migrants work in many different countries
Exchange rate shocks: when the currency of the destination country appreciates against the Philippine peso, the same salary is worth MORE in pesos back home
These exchange rate movements are driven by global macro forces, not by individual migrant or household decisions
Instrument: exchange rate shocks specific to where a household’s migrant works

title: Migration and Development
text:
Data


Panel of ~1,600 Filipino households with migrants abroad
Track household spending, education enrollment, entrepreneurial activity
Match each household to the destination country of their migrant
Observe exchange rate changes over time

title: Migration and Development
text:
Results: Investment in Education


Positive exchange rate shocks (bigger remittances) lead to significantly MORE spending on education
Children in recipient households are more likely to stay in school
The effect is concentrated in households with school-age children

title: Migration and Development
text:
Results: Entrepreneurship


Households receiving larger remittances are more likely to start small businesses
More hours worked in self-employment
Remittances are functioning as startup capital

title: Migration and Development
text:
Results: NOT Just Consumption


The increase in investment is NOT just an increase in overall spending
Households shift the COMPOSITION of their spending toward productive investment
This is the key finding: remittances change behavior, not just income

title: Migration and Development
text:
Mechanisms


Why investment rather than consumption?
Remittances relax credit constraints: families couldn’t borrow to send kids to school or start a business, but now they can
This is a story about market failures in developing countries: if credit markets worked, families would already be investing

title: Migration and Development
text:
What Do We Learn?


Migration generates massive financial flows to developing countries
These flows fund human capital and entrepreneurship, not just consumption
Remittances may be doing more for development than foreign aid
But remember: only families who can send migrants abroad benefit

title: Migration and Development
text:
Migration as Development Policy


If migration is this effective at reducing poverty and increasing investment, should development policy focus on enabling migration?
Remittances dwarf foreign aid: should we facilitate movement rather than send money?
If poverty causes conflict (MSS) and remittances alleviate poverty, could facilitating migration help prevent conflict?
But migration is politically toxic in destination countries: how do you square the development case with domestic politics?

title: Migration and Development
text:
Discussion


Yang shows remittances fund education, but the most educated people leave. Is migration a net positive or negative for origin countries?
Migration requires resources: the poorest can’t move. Does this make migration a regressive development tool?
How does this connect to the conflict classes: displacement as forced migration vs economic migration as choice?

Myth 2: Most migrants are refugees


Of ~281 million international migrants, ~36 million are refugees or asylum seekers (~13%, UNHCR 2023)
The vast majority migrate for economic reasons: labor, family reunification, education
Forced and economic migration are often intertwined: conflict destroys livelihoods
But the political debate focuses almost entirely on refugees and asylum



Why does this distinction matter for policy?

title: Migration and Development
text:
Myth 3: The poorest people migrate


Migration requires resources: savings, networks, information
The people trapped in the worst poverty often can’t move
Migrants tend to be younger, healthier, more educated, more risk-tolerant
Migration is a development tool that doesn’t reach the people who need it most

title: Migration and Development
text: Myth 4: Migration drains origin countries

title: Migration and Development
text:
Myth 4: Migration drains origin countries


Remittances to low and middle-income countries exceeded $600 billion in 2022 (World Bank)
For many countries, remittances are the largest source of foreign income
Emigration of skilled workers (“brain drain”) is a concern: ~77% of tertiary-educated adults from Haiti live abroad (Docquier and Rapoport 2012)
But diaspora networks, return migration, and remittance-funded education can generate “brain gain”

title: Migration and Development
text:
The Place Premium
Clemens, Montenegro, and Pritchett (2008) estimate the wage gap for observably identical workers across borders:


A Bolivian worker earns 3x more just by working in the US
A Nigerian worker earns 7x more
These gaps dwarf returns to education, capital, or any other intervention
The biggest price distortion in the world economy is on wages!



So why doesn’t everyone move?

title: Migration and Development
text:
Does poverty cause migration?
What do you think?

The conventional wisdom in policy circles: development reduces migration

Bill Clinton on NAFTA: “as the benefits of economic growth are spread in Mexico … there will be less illegal immigration” (White House 1993)
EU Commission (2008): migration policy should “focus much more on … improving the socio-economic situation in low-income and middle-income countries”

title: Migration and Development
text:
The Mobility Transition
Clemens (2014) reviews 45 years of evidence:


At low incomes, the ability effect dominates: development makes migration more affordable \(\rightarrow\) emigration rises
Only after ~PPP $7,000-8,000 does the incentive effect kick in: wages at home are high enough that fewer people want to leave
Result: an inverted-U between development and emigration

title: Migration and Development
text:
The Mobility Transition
Clemens (2014) reviews 45 years of evidence:


Emigration rises with income among low and lower-middle-income countries
The relationship only reverses around PPP $7,000-8,000 (upper-middle income)
Even the richest countries do not have lower emigration than the poorest
Development does not reduce migration — at least not for decades



Why? Migration requires resources: savings, networks, information. The poorest cannot afford to leave.

title: Migration and Development
text:
Forced vs Voluntary


Forced: conflict, persecution, disaster (refugees, asylum seekers, IDPs)
Voluntary: economic opportunity, family reunification, education
Of ~281 million international migrants, ~36 million are refugees or asylum seekers (~13%, UNHCR 2023)
Is the difference btw forced and voluntary clear cut?

title: Migration and Development
text: Myth 3: Migration drains origin countries

title: Migration and Development
text:
Myth 3: Migration drains origin countries


Remittances to low and middle-income countries exceeded $600 billion in 2022 (World Bank)
For many countries, remittances are the largest source of foreign income
Emigration of skilled workers is a concern: ~77% of tertiary-educated adults from Haiti live abroad (Docquier and Rapoport 2012)
But diaspora networks, return migration, and remittance-funded education can offset losses

title: Migration and Development
text:
The Opportunity Cost of Staying


Same logic as the conflict literature: people weigh costs and benefits
The opportunity cost of staying is the wage you could earn elsewhere
If wages at home are low, the returns to migration are enormous
Migration is an investment: pay upfront costs now, earn returns later



So does that mean the poorest people migrate?

title: Migration and Development
text:
What do you think?
If migration is driven by opportunity cost, should the poorest people be the most likely to migrate?

The conventional wisdom in policy circles says yes — and that development will reduce migration

Bill Clinton on NAFTA: “as the benefits of economic growth are spread in Mexico … there will be less illegal immigration” (White House 1993)
EU Commission (2008): migration policy should “focus much more on … improving the socio-economic situation in low-income and middle-income countries”

title: Migration and Development
text:
Two Competing Models
Neoclassical model (Ravenstein 1885, Lewis 1954, Harris and Todaro 1970):


Migration is an investment: move from worse circumstances to better ones
Higher income at home raises the reservation wage \(\rightarrow\) less incentive to move
Prediction: rising incomes strictly reduce emigration
Same logic as opportunity cost in the conflict literature



But what if rising incomes also change other things?

text: Macro Evidence: The Migration Hump

title: Migration and Development
text:
What the Data Show
Clemens (2014) reviews 45 years of evidence:


Emigration rises with income among low and lower-middle-income countries
The relationship only reverses around PPP $7,000-8,000 (upper-middle income)
Even the richest countries do not have lower emigration than the poorest
Development does not reduce migration — at least not for decades



The poorest cannot afford to leave. Migration requires resources: savings, networks, information.

title: Migration and Development
section: Does that mean migrants move to the richest countries?
text:
Does that mean migrants move to the richest countries?
What would you predict?

Not necessarily.

title: Migration and Development
text: South-South Migration

title: Migration and Development
text:
South-South Migration


South-South migration (105M) is larger than South-North (82M) (UN DESA 2020)
Most migration happens between neighboring countries, not across continents
Afghan refugees go to Iran and Pakistan, not Germany
Proximity, language, networks, and lower barriers matter more than wage gaps

title: Migration and Development
text:
The Scale of Remittances


Remittances to low and middle-income countries exceeded $600 billion in 2022 (World Bank)
For many countries, remittances are the largest source of foreign income
Emigration of skilled workers is a concern: ~77% of tertiary-educated adults from Haiti live abroad (Docquier and Rapoport 2012)
But diaspora networks, return migration, and remittance-funded education can offset losses



So what do families actually do with remittance money? This is what Yang (2008) studies.

title: Migration and Development
text:
Migrants Are Not Random


Migrants are not a random sample of the origin population
They tend to be younger, healthier, more educated, more risk-tolerant
This creates a measurement problem: if we compare migrants to non-migrants, we’re comparing different kinds of people
Sound familiar? (Connect to selection bias in Blattman and Annan)

title: Migration and Development
text:
Migration as Investment
If migration is an investment, not everyone can afford it:


Moving costs money: transport, visas, fees, settling in a new place
You need information: where to go, how to get there, who can help
You need networks: a cousin, a friend, a community at the destination
The poorest people have the most to gain but cannot pay the upfront cost

title: Migration and Development
text:
Two Forces
So what happens as countries develop?


More financial reason to stay: wages at home rise, the gap with abroad shrinks
But easier to leave: people can afford the trip, transport is cheaper, diaspora networks grow, information flows improve



Which effect dominates?

title: Migration and Development
section: Remittances Are Huge — But Are They Productive?
text:
Remittances Are Huge — But Are They Productive?


Remittances exceeded $600 billion in 2022 — larger than all foreign aid (World Bank)
But money alone doesn’t guarantee development
Do families spend it on consumption (food, goods) or investment (education, business)?



This is what Yang (2008) studies.

title: Migration and Development
text:
Selection Problem


Migrants are not a random sample of the origin population
They tend to be younger, healthier, more educated, more risk-tolerant
This creates a measurement problem: if we compare migrants to non-migrants, we’re comparing different kinds of people
Sound familiar? (Connect to selection bias in Blattman and Annan)

title: Migration and Development
text:
The Instrument in Detail
Yang uses the 1997 Asian financial crisis:


Some currencies appreciated against the peso (USD, Saudi riyal) \(\rightarrow\) remittances worth more
Others depreciated (Malaysian ringgit, HK dollar) \(\rightarrow\) remittances worth less
Each household gets a different shock depending on where their migrant works
Which country the migrant went to was decided before the crisis — not a response to it

title: Migration and Development
text:
Identifying Assumptions
Instrument valid if exchange rate shocks are unrelated to household type


Threat: richer households send migrants to dollar-pegged countries \(\rightarrow\) controls for pre-crisis household characteristics
Threat: crisis changes labor demand, migrants come home \(\rightarrow\) shows return rates don’t differ across destinations
Key: variation comes from which currency your migrant earns in, decided before the crisis

title: Text as Data
text:
What is a latent variable?

A quantity we care about that we cannot directly observe. We infer it from things we can measure.




State capacity inferred from tax-to-GDP ratio, public goods provision, bureaucratic retention


Electoral fraud inferred from digit patterns in vote tallies, turnout discontinuities, vote-share heaping


Ethnic polarization inferred from residential segregation, cross-ethnic voting, intermarriage patterns




The proxy is observable. The latent variable is not. We use the former to reason about the latter.

title: Text as Data
section: Text as a window into latent states
text:
Text as a window into latent states

Text is produced by people and institutions. What they write is shaped by what they believe, want, and feel.


We posit that the text we observe is a product of latent states we care about:




Legislative capture do legislators’ floor speeches echo their donors’ interests? word choice says yes


Pre-violence hostility dehumanizing language in Rwandan radio preceded the 1994 genocide by months


Policy sincerity gap between donor-facing reports and domestic budget speeches reveals actual priorities




Same logic as any other measurement problem. Different observable.

title: Text as Data
text:
Text as a trace

Actors have beliefs, interests, and intentions that shape what they write but we cannot observe directly



Ideology: party manifestos
Hostility: dehumanizing language

title: Text as Data
text:
The data generating process


Latent variable ideology, sentiment, priorities, hostility


↓


Language generation word choice, framing, emphasis, omission


↓


Observed text speeches, reports, manifestos, tweets


↑


We only observe this. We want to infer upward.

title: Text as Data
text:
What we want to measure


Sentiment / Tone: how positive, negative, or hostile is this document?
Topic: what is this document about?
Position: where does this actor sit in some ideological space?
Similarity: are these two documents saying the same thing? written by the same person?

title: Text as Data
text:
From words to numbers


Corpus: collection of documents and metadata
Tokenize: split into units (words, n-grams)
Preprocess: remove stopwords, punctuation, normalize case
Document-Term Matrix: rows = documents, columns = terms, cells = counts
Model: apply a method to recover the latent quantity

title: Text as Data
text:
Four families of methods


Dictionary methods: researcher defines a word list; score documents by counts. Fast, transparent, brittle.
Supervised models: hand-code a sample; train a classifier to generalize. Flexible, requires labeled data.
Unsupervised models: let the model find structure without labels. Scalable, hard to validate.
Large language models: pretrained on massive corpora; prompted or fine-tuned. Powerful, opaque, expensive, hard to validate systematically.

title: Text as Data
text:
Enter quanteda

quanteda is an R package that handles the entire pipeline



Corpus management: store documents with metadata, filter, subset
Tokenization and preprocessing in one step
Fast, sparse document-term matrix construction
Built-in methods: KWIC, wordclouds, dictionary scoring, scaling models, topic models



It is not the only option, but it is well-documented, actively maintained, and designed for social scientists


Let’s go to R.

title: Gender and Development
text:
The Research Question
Does mandated representation of women change policy outcomes?


Reserved positions assigned by random lottery
Do villages with female heads invest differently than those with male heads?

title: Gender and Development
text:
Theory
Hypothesis: Reserved villages invest more in goods women prioritize


Mechanism: Heterogeneous priorities

Women and men have different policy preferences
Female leaders translate those preferences into policy

If true: representation has substantive, not just symbolic, value

title: Gender and Development
text:
Research Design
Treatment: Village council randomly assigned a female head (reserved seat lottery)


Identification: Randomization via lottery

Reserved vs. non-reserved villages are comparable on all other dimensions

Outcome: Public investment decisions (type and quantity)
Data: Village councils in West Bengal and Rajasthan, India

title: Gender and Development
text:
From Math to Software
Recall the partial derivative:
\[\frac{\partial Y}{\partial X} = \beta_1 + \beta_3 \cdot Z\]

When quota_system = 0: effect of women_representation = \(\beta_1\)
When quota_system = 1: effect of women_representation = \(\beta_1 + \beta_3\)


The marginaleffects package computes this for you – at every observation, then summarizes

title: Gender and Development
text:
Marginal Effects with marginaleffects

library(marginaleffects)

# Marginal effect of women_representation, by quota_system
slopes(interaction_model,
       variables = "women_representation",
       by = "quota_system")


                 Term quota_system Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)    S
 women_representation            0   -0.487      0.229 -2.13   0.0336  4.9
 women_representation            1    2.405      0.318  7.55   <0.001 44.4
  2.5 %  97.5 %
 -0.935 -0.0379
  1.781  3.0286

Type:  response 
Columns: term, quota_system, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value, s.value, conf.low, conf.high

title: Gender and Development
text: Plot Marginal Effects

title: Gender and Development
text:
What Did We Just Do?

slopes() evaluated \(\beta_1 + \beta_3 \cdot Z\) at each level of quota_system
Without quota: effect of representation is negative (\(\beta_1 = -0.5\))
With quota: effect flips positive (\(\beta_1 + \beta_3 = -0.5 + 3 = 2.5\))


This is exactly what we derived on paper – marginaleffects just does the arithmetic and gives you uncertainty estimates too

Gender and Representation

Women hold only 27.0% of legislative seats (IPU, 2023)
23% of cabinet positions (UNWOMEN)
Disputed gender gap in turnout, large variance

title: Gender and Development
text:
Gender and Development

Female labor force participation rate: ~47% vs. ~73% male (ILO, 2023)
Gender wage gap (Pew)
1/3 of women have experienced GBV

title: Gender and Development
text:
Measuring \(D_i\): Gender Differences in Requests

Authors surveyed villagers: “Have you made a request to the GP in the past 6 months?”
Requests = complaints or petitions for specific public goods (water, roads, irrigation…)
For each good \(i\), \(D_i\) = share of women requesting it minus share of men requesting it
Positive \(D_i\): women want it more. Negative: men want it more.

title: Gender and Development
text:
Marginal Effects: The Idea
Recall:
\[\frac{\partial Y}{\partial X} = \beta_1 + \beta_3 \cdot Z\]

The effect of \(X\) on \(Y\) is not a single number – it depends on \(Z\)
marginaleffects evaluates this at specified values of \(Z\) and computes uncertainty


Two cases: \(Z\) is binary vs. \(Z\) is continuous

title: Gender and Development
text:
Binary Moderator: Two Estimates

slopes(model_binary,
       variables = "women_rep",
       by = "quota")

 women_rep     0   -0.547      0.177 -3.1  0.00194   9.0 -0.893 -0.201
 women_rep     1    2.351      0.185 12.7  < 0.001 120.6  1.989  2.714

title: Gender and Development
section: Continuous Moderator: A Line, Not Two Points
text:
Continuous Moderator: A Line, Not Two Points
When \(Z\) is continuous, the marginal effect varies across the full range of \(Z\)

Back to C&D logic: as \(D_i\) increases (women want a good more relative to men), does the effect of reservation on investment grow?

title: Gender and Development
text:
What to Look For
Binary moderator - Two point estimates with CIs – does the effect change sign or magnitude?
Continuous moderator - A line with CI band – where does the effect become significant? Where does it flip?

Both are \(\beta_1 + \beta_3 \cdot Z\) evaluated at different values of \(Z\) – marginaleffects handles the standard errors

title: Health and Development
text:
The Perils of RDD


You estimate a local effect – units right at the cutoff, not the full population
The cutoff is often arbitrary: cities near the Huai River may not represent all of China
If the cutoff region is unrepresentative, external validity is limited
RDD answers: “what happens just at the threshold?” – which may be of little theoretical interest

title: Health and Development
text:
Does Development Make Us Healthier?
Why we might think yes:


Vaccines and antibiotics eliminated mass killers
Sanitation and clean water cut infectious disease
Better nutrition reduced stunting and mortality
Heating reduced cold-related deaths
Richer states can fund hospitals, doctors, public health

title: Health and Development
text:
Discussion
What is the counterfactual?


The heating policy killed people through pollution
But without free coal, people in northern China faced brutal winters
Did the policy kill more people than it saved from freezing?
How do you even evaluate a policy like this?



This is the fundamental challenge of policy evaluation: the counterfactual is never observed

Agenda

Climate and Development
Dell, Jones & Olken (2012)
Interpreting Logged Variables

title: Climate and Development
text: The Planet Is Warming

title: Climate and Development
text: The Poorest Bear the Most

title: Climate and Development
section: Why Should We Expect Climate to Affect Development?
text:
Why Should We Expect Climate to Affect Development?


Agriculture: crop yields fall as temperatures rise above optimal thresholds
Labor productivity: heat stress reduces output, especially outdoor work
Health: heat-related illness, disease vector expansion (malaria, dengue)
Conflict: resource scarcity and stress increase violence
Infrastructure: extreme weather destroys capital

title: Climate and Development
text:
But Rich Countries Seem Fine


Most rich countries are in temperate climates
Is that a coincidence?
Or have they adapted – air conditioning, irrigated agriculture, insurance markets?
Key question: is the effect of temperature the same everywhere, or does it depend on income?

title: Climate and Development
text:
The Research Question
Does temperature affect economic growth? Does the effect differ by income?


Cross-country pattern: hot countries are poor
But that correlation cannot support causal inference
Hot countries differ in colonization history, institutions, geography, disease burden…
Need a cleaner source of variation

title: Climate and Development
text:
Theory
If temperature does affect growth, where would we expect to see it most?


Places with less capacity to adapt: rain-fed agriculture, weak health systems, fragile institutions
So … poor countries

title: Climate and Development
text:
Research Design
Key insight: year-to-year temperature fluctuations are plausibly exogenous


A country’s average temperature is confounded with history, geography, institutions
But whether this year was hotter than usual is essentially random – weather
Identification assumption: temperature deviations from a country’s long-run norm affect growth only through economic channels

title: Climate and Development
text:
Data

Temperature and precipitation: gridded weather station data, 125 countries, 1950–2003
Economic growth: GDP per capita growth (Penn World Tables)
Unit of analysis: country-year
Separate estimates for rich and poor countries (above/below median income in 1970)

title: Climate and Development
text:
The Model
\[\Delta \ln y_{it} = \beta_1 T_{it} + \beta_2 P_{it} + \alpha_i + \gamma_t + \epsilon_{it}\]
Where:

\(\Delta \ln y_{it}\) is GDP per capita growth in country \(i\), year \(t\)
\(T_{it}\) is mean annual temperature (deviation from country mean)
\(P_{it}\) is annual precipitation
\(\alpha_i\) are country fixed effects – absorb all time-invariant country factors
\(\gamma_t\) are year fixed effects – absorb global shocks

title: Climate and Development
text:
Main Findings


In poor countries: a 1C increase above a country’s own average in a given year reduces growth by 1.3 percentage points
In rich countries: no significant effect
Effects appear across agriculture, industry, and investment
Precipitation: no robust effect

title: Climate and Development
text:
Mechanisms


Agricultural output falls sharply – poor countries depend heavily on rain-fed crops
Industrial output also declines – labor productivity channel
Investment falls – firms anticipate lower returns
Political instability rises – more leadership transitions in hot years



No single channel dominates. Temperature hits the whole economy simultaneously.

title: Climate and Development
section: What This Means for Climate Change
text:
What This Means for Climate Change


These are transitory shocks – climate change means permanently higher temperatures
If poor countries cannot grow their way out of heat, the development gap widens
Adaptation matters: the rich-poor gap in sensitivity suggests it is possible – but costly
Mitigation vs. adaptation: a tradeoff developing countries did not create

title: Climate and Development
text:
What Is Panel Data?

Observations on the same units (countries, firms, individuals) over time
Gives us two dimensions of variation: across units and within units over time


Why does this matter?
Units differ in many ways we cannot measure – history, culture, geography. Panel data lets us hold those constant.

title: Climate and Development
text:
The Fixed Effects Idea


Each country has a fixed effect \(\alpha_i\) – its own intercept
This absorbs everything about a country that does not change over time
We identify the effect of temperature from deviations within each country relative to its own average
A hot year in Sweden vs. a normal year in Sweden – not Sweden vs. Nigeria

title: Climate and Development
text:
The Model Again
\[\Delta \ln y_{it} = \beta_1 T_{it} + \beta_2 P_{it} + \alpha_i + \gamma_t + \epsilon_{it}\]

\(\alpha_i\): country FE – controls for all time-invariant confounders (geography, colonial history…)
\(\gamma_t\): year FE – controls for global shocks (oil price, global recession…)
\(\hat{\beta}_1\): identified from within-country variation in temperature over time

title: Climate and Development
text:
In R: fixest

# install.packages("fixest")
library(fixest)

# Two-way fixed effects: country + year
model <- feols(gdp_growth ~ temperature + precipitation | country + year,
               data = panel_data,
               cluster = ~country)

summary(model)



| country + year: the fixed effects
cluster = ~country: standard errors clustered at the country level (why?)

title: Climate and Development
text:
Simulating Panel FE


Show code
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)
set.seed(42)

n_countries <- 30
n_years     <- 20

panel <- expand_grid(country = 1:n_countries, year = 1:n_years) %>%
  mutate(
    country_fe  = rep(rnorm(n_countries, 0, 2), each = n_years),
    temperature = rnorm(n(), 0, 1),
    gdp_growth  = 2 + (-1.3) * temperature + country_fe + rnorm(n(), 0, 1)
  )

# Naive OLS -- biased if country_fe correlates with temperature
ols  <- lm(gdp_growth ~ temperature, data = panel)

# Two-way FE -- consistent
twfe <- feols(gdp_growth ~ temperature | country + year, data = panel)

cat("OLS estimate:", round(coef(ols)["temperature"], 3),
    "\nFE estimate:",  round(coef(twfe)["temperature"], 3),
    "\nTrue effect:  -1.3")


OLS estimate: -1.46 
FE estimate: -1.298 
True effect:  -1.3

title: Climate and Development
text:
Why FE vs. OLS?


OLS estimate is biased: conflates within-country temperature variation with between-country differences
Country FE removes the between-country variation – identifies from within only
The difference between the two estimates is the confounding from time-invariant country characteristics
This is why Dell et al. cannot simply compare hot countries to cold countries

title: Climate and Development
text:
The Limits of Panel FE


Removes all time-invariant confounders – but not time-varying ones
Key assumption: no omitted variable that varies within a country over time and correlates with temperature
Cannot tell us about long-run effects of permanently higher temperature (only year-to-year shocks)
Generalization from short-run shocks to long-run climate change requires additional assumptions

title: Climate and Development

title: Climate and Development
text:
Why Should Climate Affect Development?


Agriculture: crop yields fall above optimal temperature thresholds
Labor productivity: heat stress reduces output, especially outdoor and manual work
Health: heat illness, expanded disease vectors (malaria, dengue)
Conflict: resource scarcity increases stress and violence
Infrastructure: extreme weather destroys capital

title: Climate and Development
text:
But Rich Countries Seem Unaffected


Most wealthy countries are in temperate climates
Many have adapted: air conditioning, irrigated agriculture, crop switching, insurance markets
Key question: is the effect of temperature the same everywhere, or does it depend on income?

title: Climate and Development
text: The Identification Problem

title: Climate and Development
text:
Data and Model
125 countries, 1950–2003. Temperature from gridded weather data. GDP growth from Penn World Tables.
\[\Delta \ln y_{it} = \beta_1 T_{it} + \beta_2 P_{it} + \alpha_i + \gamma_t + \epsilon_{it}\]

\(T_{it}\): mean temperature in country \(i\), year \(t\), relative to that country’s mean over the full sample (1950–2003)
\(\alpha_i\): country fixed effects
\(\gamma_t\): year fixed effects

title: Climate and Development
text:
Heterogeneous Effects Are an Interaction
The rich vs. poor split is a modeling decision, not just a narrative
\[\Delta \ln y_{it} = \beta_1 T_{it} + \beta_2 \text{Poor}_i + \beta_3 (T_{it} \times \text{Poor}_i) + \alpha_i + \gamma_t + \epsilon_{it}\]


\(\beta_1\): effect of temperature in rich countries
\(\beta_1 + \beta_3\): effect of temperature in poor countries
\(\beta_3\): does temperature hit poor countries harder?
The marginal effect of \(T\) depends on income – exactly the interaction structure you know

title: Climate and Development
text:
The Extrapolation Problem
Dell et al. identify effects from year-to-year shocks. Climate change is permanent. These are different.


Short-run: no time to adapt – crops, firms, and governments are stuck
Long-run: adaptation is possible

Short-run estimates may overstate damage if adaptation works
May understate it if capital degrades irreversibly

Dell et al. test with 10-year windows: effect is smaller but persists
Short-run estimates are credible; translating to permanent warming requires further assumptions

title: Climate and Development
section: Can We Fix the Extrapolation Problem?
text:
Can We Fix the Extrapolation Problem?


One approach: long differences – look at 10-year average temperature vs. 10-year growth

Allows some adaptation, still uses variation within countries
Dell et al. find the effect is smaller but still present

Another approach: compare countries that differ in climate trends over decades

Harder – confounded with other changes

Bottom line: short-run panel estimates are credible for identification, but the translation to long-run climate change requires additional assumptions

title: Climate and Development
text:
What This Means for Policy


If effects are real and large: a 2–4°C world hits poor countries hardest
The countries that emitted least are most exposed
Adaptation can reduce the damage but requires investment poor countries cannot afford
Mitigation (cutting emissions) addresses the source – but is a global public good problem
This is not just a science problem – it is a development problem

title: Climate and Development
section: Critical Thinking: The Political Instability Story
text:
Critical Thinking: The Political Instability Story


Dell et al. find more irregular leadership transitions in hotter years in poor countries
Does heat cause conflict, or do both reflect deeper fragility?
The instability result is smaller and less robust than the GDP result
Instability may be a mechanism or a consequence of worse economic outcomes – not a clean separate channel
Takeaway: mechanism identification is much harder than reduced-form identification

title: Climate and Development
text:
What the Paper Actually Argues


The rich-poor asymmetry suggests the damage from climate change will widen global inequality
Historical emissions came overwhelmingly from rich countries; damages fall on poor ones
The paper is careful: these are income effects on growth rates, not levels – compounding matters enormously
A 1.3pp drag on growth, sustained over decades, means massive foregone development
The authors do not say adaptation is impossible – but it requires investment poor countries cannot self-finance

title: Climate and Development
text:
Interpreting Log Transformations
The DV is \(\Delta \ln y_{it}\) – the log difference in GDP per capita, which approximates the growth rate.

Why does \(\ln Y\) work that way? Take the derivative:
\[\frac{d \ln Y}{d X} = \frac{1}{Y} \frac{dY}{dX} \approx \% \Delta Y\]


So when the DV is logged and \(X\) is in levels: \(\hat{\beta}\) is the percentage point change in \(Y\) per unit increase in \(X\).

title: Climate and Development
text: Main Results

title: Climate and Development
text:
Reading the Table



  

  
  
  

  
  
  

  
  
  



  
    Col (1): no effect on average across all countries.
  
  
    Col (2): temperature interacted with a poor country dummy. Large and significant (-1.655***).
  
  
    Marginal effect in poor countries: β_temp + β_interaction = -1.4pp. Same logic as slopes().

title: Climate and Development
text:
Log-Log and Level-Log
When both are logged – the elasticity case:
\[\ln Y = \alpha + \beta \ln X \implies \frac{d \ln Y}{d \ln X} = \beta \implies \hat{\beta} = \frac{\% \Delta Y}{\% \Delta X}\]
A 1% increase in \(X\) leads to a \(\hat{\beta}\)% change in \(Y\).

When only \(X\) is logged:
\[Y = \alpha + \beta \ln X \implies \frac{dY}{d \ln X} = \beta \implies \hat{\beta} \approx \frac{\Delta Y}{1\% \Delta X / 100}\]
A 1% increase in \(X\) leads to a \(\hat{\beta}/100\) unit change in \(Y\).

title: Climate and Development
text:
What the Paper Argues


The rich-poor asymmetry suggests climate change will widen global inequality
Historical emissions came overwhelmingly from rich countries; damages fall on poor ones
These are effects on growth rates, not levels; compounding matters enormously
A 1.3pp drag sustained over decades means massive foregone development
Adaptation is possible but requires investment poor countries cannot self-finance

title: Climate and Development
text:
Log-Level: DV is Logged
The DV is \(\Delta \ln y_{it}\) – the log difference in GDP, which approximates the growth rate.

Why? Take the derivative of \(\ln Y = \alpha + \beta X\):
\[\frac{d \ln Y}{d X} = \frac{1}{Y} \frac{dY}{dX} \approx \% \Delta Y\]


So \(\hat{\beta}\) is the percentage point change in \(Y\) per one unit increase in \(X\).
In Dell et al.: \(\hat{\beta} = -0.013\) means 1°C above normal reduces GDP growth by 1.3 percentage points.

title: Climate and Development
text:
Level-Log: X is Logged
When only \(X\) is logged:
\[Y = \alpha + \beta \ln X\]
\[\frac{dY}{d \ln X} = \beta \implies \hat{\beta} \approx \frac{\Delta Y}{1\% \Delta X / 100}\]
A 1% increase in \(X\) leads to a \(\hat{\beta}/100\) unit change in \(Y\).

Common in wage regressions: \(\text{wage} = \alpha + \beta \ln(\text{experience})\)

title: Climate and Development
text:
Log-Log: Both Logged (Elasticity)
\[\ln Y = \alpha + \beta \ln X \implies \frac{d \ln Y}{d \ln X} = \beta\]
\(\hat{\beta}\) is the elasticity: a 1% increase in \(X\) leads to a \(\hat{\beta}\)% change in \(Y\).

Common in trade and demand models. Useful when the relationship is proportional.

title: Climate and Development
text:
A Quick Calculus Reminder
For the natural log and exponential:
\[\frac{d}{dX} \ln X = \frac{1}{X} \qquad \frac{d}{dX} e^X = e^X\]

The key insight: differences in logs are approximately percent changes

For small changes, \(\ln(Y_2) - \ln(Y_1) \approx \% \Delta Y\). Exact for big changes, approximate for small ones.

title: Climate and Development
text:
Summary









\(Y\) in levels
\(Y\) logged




\(X\) in levels
\(\hat\beta\): unit change in \(Y\)
\(\hat\beta \times 100\): % change in \(Y\)


\(X\) logged
\(\hat\beta/100\): unit change per 1% \(\uparrow X\)
\(\hat\beta\): % change per 1% \(\uparrow X\)

title: Climate and Development
text:
Why This Matters for Regression
If your DV is logged: \(\ln Y = \alpha + \beta X\)

A one-unit increase in \(X\) changes \(\ln Y\) by \(\hat\beta\) – which is approximately a \(\hat\beta \times 100\)% change in \(Y\).


In Dell et al.: \(\hat\beta = -0.013\) – a 1°C shock reduces GDP by approximately 1.3% – which here is 1.3 percentage points of growth.

title: Climate and Development
text:
If X is Logged
\(Y = \alpha + \beta \ln X\) – a 1% increase in \(X\) changes \(\ln X\) by about 0.01, so \(Y\) changes by \(\hat\beta \times 0.01 = \hat\beta/100\) units.

Common example: wages and years of experience. Each additional 1% of experience adds \(\hat\beta/100\) dollars.

\(\ln Y = \alpha + \beta \ln X\) – a 1% increase in \(X\) leads to a \(\hat\beta\)% change in \(Y\).
This is called an elasticity – common in trade and demand models.

Two common cases:

Finding: Heat and Political Instability
Dell et al. also find: hotter years in poor countries see more irregular leadership transitions

What does this tell us about mechanism?

If heat causes conflict → conflict tanks the economy → instability is a channel
If heat tanks the economy → weak states collapse → instability is a symptom
If poor, fragile states are hit hardest by everything → instability and GDP loss are both consequences



The instability result is smaller and less robust than the GDP result. Does that change your interpretation?

title: Climate and Development
text:
Should Climate Change Affect Development?


Agriculture: crop yields fall above optimal temperature thresholds
Labor productivity: heat stress reduces output, especially outdoor and manual work
Health: heat illness, expanded disease vectors (malaria, dengue)
Conflict: resource scarcity increases stress and violence
Infrastructure: extreme weather destroys capital

title: Climate and Development
text: Hot Countries Are Poor

title: Climate and Development
text:
What Do You Notice?


Hotter places tend to be poorer. Does that mean heat causes poverty?
What else differs between Nigeria and Norway besides temperature?
Colonization history, institutions, geography, disease burden, trade access…
The cross-country pattern cannot isolate the effect of temperature

title: Climate and Development
text:
The Clever Fix


Compare each country to itself over time, not to other countries
Country fixed effects absorb everything time-invariant (geography, history, institutions)
Year fixed effects absorb global shocks
Why deviations from the long-run mean? Raw temperature + country FE would work algebraically, but we need a benchmark for “normal.” The sample average (1950-2003) is pre-climate-change: it tells us what was typical for each country before the trend began
So the question becomes: was this year unusually hot for this country? That’s weather, essentially random
Identification assumption: year-to-year temperature shocks affect growth only through economic channels

title: Climate and Development
text:
Why Deviations from the Mean?


Country FE already absorb time-invariant differences, so we are comparing each country to itself
But what counts as “normal” for that country? We need a pre-climate-change benchmark
The sample average (1950-2003) serves as that baseline: it reflects each country’s historical climate before the trend shifted
So \(T_{it}\) asks: was this year unusually hot for this country? That is weather, essentially random
Identification assumption: year-to-year temperature shocks affect growth only through economic channels

Country and Year FE absorb everything time-invariant for the country and year including “climate”
\(T_{it}\) measures was this year unusually hot for this country? Weather
Identification assumption: conditional on country and year FE, year-to-year temperature fluctuations are uncorrelated with other determinants of GDP growth (i.e., \(T_{it}\) is exogenous)

section: What Is Aid Supposed to Do?
text:
What Is Aid Supposed to Do?


Fill a savings gap: poor countries cannot accumulate enough capital on their own
Finance public goods: roads, health systems, courts that no private actor will build
Buffer shocks: drought, conflict, pandemic relief
Build institutions: training, technical assistance, governance support

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Why Might Aid Not Work?


Fungibility: recipients shift their own budgets away from aided sectors, leaving total spending unchanged
Weak absorption: money arrives but cannot be spent productively given limited capacity
Donor incentives: aid flows for strategic and political reasons, not only development ones
Dutch disease: large inflows appreciate the exchange rate, hurting exports

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
The Big Question


Four decades of research. Similar data. Wildly different answers.
Some studies find aid robustly raises growth. Others find zero. Others find effects only under the right conditions.
Is the disagreement real, or is something going wrong with the measurement and methods?

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Four Decades, Three Answers


Boone (1996): no effect on investment or growth across 96 countries
Burnside & Dollar (2000): aid raises growth, but only with good policy
Rajan & Subramanian (2008): no robust effect, even with good policy
Similar data, similar periods, three different conclusions

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
What Do You Notice?


All three measure aggregate foreign aid as the treatment variable
All three use instrumental variables to address reverse causation
All three reach different conclusions
If the same data yield such different answers, something is wrong with how the question is being framed

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Two Problems

Problem 1: Timing. Not all aid is the same. Road construction may raise output for decades. A vaccination campaign yields health benefits over a generation. Humanitarian food relief may never affect GDP. Lumping all aid together and testing for immediate growth effects is a category error.
Problem 2: Instruments. All three studies instrument for aid using country size and political ties to donors. Across all three, population size is responsible for nearly all the identification strength. Population affects growth through many channels unrelated to aid.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
section: Problem 1: Not All Aid Is Growth Aid
text:
Problem 1: Not All Aid Is Growth Aid


Early-impact aid

Budget and program support
Infrastructure: roads, energy, communications, banking
Productive sectors: agriculture, industry

Plausible growth effect within a few years

Excluded from early-impact

Technical cooperation
Education and health
Humanitarian and food aid
Democracy and governance programs
Administrative overhead

Growth effects, if any, arrive much later or never


Early-impact aid accounts for roughly 45 to 53% of total flows.
