title: Foreign Aid and Development
section: Why Is Population a Bad Instrument?
text:
Why Is Population a Bad Instrument?


Larger countries receive less aid as a share of GDP, so population correlates with aid
Population also affects growth through trade, market size, economies of scale, and political stability
For population to be a valid instrument, it must affect growth only through the aid channel
That exclusion restriction is not credible
Any one of those alternative channels invalidates the whole IV strategy

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text: The Causal Challenge

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
The Fix: Three Steps


Lag aid: test whether Aid(t-1) predicts Growth(t). A country’s growth this period cannot have caused its aid receipts last period. This severs the contemporaneous reverse causation channel.
First-difference: subtract each country’s previous-period values from the current period. Time-invariant traits like geography or colonial history drop out. Omitted variable bias from fixed country characteristics is eliminated.
Restrict to early-impact aid: drop flows with no plausible near-term growth mechanism. What remains is the subset that has a theoretical reason to affect GDP within the study window.



No IV needed. Lagging and differencing do the identification work.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
What They Find


Results consistent across all three reanalyzed datasets
+1 pp in Aid/GDP is followed on average by:

+0.1 to 0.2 pp in annual real GDP per capita growth
+0.3 to 0.5 pp in Investment/GDP

Positive but modest; diminishing returns set in and the effect turns negative at high aid levels

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Diminishing Returns


Aid-growth relationship is non-linear: adding a quadratic term for aid substantially improves fit
The marginal return to aid declines with aid intensity
The turning point varies by specification: roughly 5 to 22% of GDP
Beyond that point, additional aid is associated with lower growth
Interpretation: institutions and absorptive capacity constrain how productively a country can use external resources

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
What About Boone’s Null Result?


Boone dropped all countries receiving more than 15% of GNI in aid from his baseline sample
He argued these countries are outliers where aid is non-fungible
CRBB show this restriction is not justified statistically and biases the result
With the full sample, even Boone’s own contemporaneous OLS specification shows a positive and significant effect of aid on investment
The null result was a sample restriction artifact, not a finding about aid

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
What About Causation?


CRBB find Granger causation: lagged aid predicts future growth after controlling for past growth
This is not the same as strict causal identification from a randomized experiment
Reverse causation cannot be fully ruled out even with lagging
The authors test two specific alternative mechanisms (donor foresight about future growth, mean reversion) and find limited support for either
Their argument: a positive signal appears consistently across three independent datasets and many specification checks. Coincidence is less plausible than a real effect.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
What the Paper Argues


Aid causes some growth on average: modest, with wide variation across recipients
High aid dependence shows diminishing returns; it cannot substitute for domestic investment

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
What Is Aid For?


Fill a savings gap: poor countries cannot accumulate enough capital on their own
Finance public goods: roads, health systems, courts that no private actor will build
Buffer shocks: drought, conflict, pandemic relief
Build institutions: training, technical assistance, governance support

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Does Foreign Aid Cause Growth?


Over 60 years, rich countries have transferred trillions of dollars to poor ones
Governments, NGOs, and international organizations make allocation decisions based on the answer
So: what does the evidence say?

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Why Do They Disagree?


These studies overlap substantially in countries, years, and data sources
CRBB argue the divergence comes from two resolvable research design choices
The first is about measurement: what counts as aid, and over what time horizon?
The second is about identification: how do you separate the effect of aid from the effect of everything that moves with aid?

title: Foreign Aid and Development
section: Question 1: When Should We See Growth?
text:
Question 1: When Should We See Growth?


A road raises productivity for decades. Food relief addresses a crisis this week.
Testing whether all aid raises GDP this year is asking whether food relief builds roads.
The time horizon should depend on what type of aid you are measuring.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
section: Question 2: Is All Aid the Same?
text:
Question 2: Is All Aid the Same?


Early-impact: budget support, roads, energy, agriculture. Plausible growth effect within a few years.
Long-horizon: education, health, technical cooperation. Growth effects arrive over a generation.
No growth mechanism: humanitarian aid, food relief, emergency assistance.



Early-impact aid is roughly 45 to 53% of total flows.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Prior Studies: Instrumental Variables


All three studies instrument for aid to address reverse causation
A valid instrument predicts Aid/GDP but affects growth only through aid
All three rely primarily on recipient country population size
Population correlates with Aid/GDP (larger countries get less per capita), but also affects growth through market size, trade, economies of scale
When CRBB remove population from the instrument set, F-statistics collapse below 2 in all three studies. Threshold for strong instrumentation: 10.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Designing a Better Study
If you were studying whether aid causes growth, what would you do?


When to measure growth: allow time for aid to translate into investment and output. Test whether Aid(t-1) predicts Growth(t).
What aid to include: restrict to flows with a plausible short-run growth mechanism. Drop humanitarian, health, education flows.
How to handle country fixed characteristics: subtract out each country’s own past values. Geography, institutions, colonial history all cancel.
Instruments: none needed. Lagging and differencing do the identification work.



This is exactly what CRBB do.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Is This Actually Causal?


Time-varying confounders: a crisis can simultaneously trigger more aid and hurt growth; lagging and differencing do not fully remove this
Mean reversion: bad growth attracts aid AND predicts recovery; aid may look effective simply because bad years do not persist

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
What Boone Got Wrong


Boone dropped all countries receiving more than 15% of GNI in aid, arguing they are outliers
These are precisely the most aid-dependent countries, where the effect should be most visible
CRBB show these observations are not statistical outliers and should not have been dropped
With the full sample, even Boone’s contemporaneous OLS shows a positive and significant aid-investment relationship
His null result came from the sample restriction, not from the data

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text: Aid Is Under Pressure

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Who Gets Hurt?


Countries where aid is 10 to 20% of GDP face acute fiscal shortfalls with no capacity to absorb them
Sub-Saharan Africa: highest aid dependence, weakest domestic revenue base
Health programs (HIV treatment, malaria, TB) face immediate disruption
Aid cuts reduce investment and remove shock buffers in the countries least able to absorb them

title: Foreign Aid and Development
section: What Does the Evidence Say We Should Expect?
text:
What Does the Evidence Say We Should Expect?


If CRBB are right, sustained aid cuts slow growth in the most dependent countries
The effect is not catastrophic in any single year but compounds: a 1pp growth drag sustained over a decade is enormous foregone development
The countries least able to replace aid with domestic revenue or private capital are the ones most exposed
This is also an opportunity to test the theory: if aid was causing growth, we should see slowdowns where cuts were sharpest

title: Foreign Aid and Development
section: Now Suppose We Measure Aid Correctly
text:
Now Suppose We Measure Aid Correctly
Even with the right measure and the right lag, we still have a problem.

Countries that receive more aid tend to be poorer, slower-growing, or in crisis. Aid and low growth travel together in the data.


How do we know whether aid is causing slow growth, or whether slow growth is causing more aid?

title: Foreign Aid and Development
section: Decision 1: When Do You Measure Growth?
text:
Decision 1: When Do You Measure Growth?
Data is averaged into 4-year periods to smooth annual noise. Aid arrives in period \(t\).


(a) Same period: current growth affects how much aid countries receive. Reverse causation.
(b) Next period: allows time for aid to work. Severs the contemporaneous feedback loop.
(c) 10 years later: plausible for infrastructure, but most of the sample disappears.



CRBB choose (b): does Aid(\(t-1\)) predict Growth(\(t\))?

title: Foreign Aid and Development
section: Decision 2: Which Aid Flows Do You Include?
text:
Decision 2: Which Aid Flows Do You Include?
Your data includes roads, food relief, vaccination programs, budget support, technical cooperation.


(a) All disbursements: maximum sample, but most flows have no short-run growth mechanism.
(b) Project aid only: misses budget support, which can fund productive investment.
(c) Only aid that could plausibly raise productive capacity within a few years: roads, energy, agriculture, budget support.



CRBB choose (c). Early-impact aid. About 45 to 53% of total flows.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
section: Decision 3: How Do You Handle Confounders?
text:
Decision 3: How Do You Handle Confounders?
Poor, conflict-prone countries attract more aid and grow more slowly.


(a) Add country controls: you cannot observe everything.
(b) First-difference: subtract each country’s own past values. Geography, institutions, colonial history cancel out.
(c) Find an instrument: prior studies used recipient country population size. Population affects growth through market size, trade, and economies of scale — not only through aid. The instrument fails.



CRBB choose (b).

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
What Is Mean Reversion?
A country has an unusually bad year. Growth collapses. Donors send emergency aid. The next year, things normalize and growth recovers.

The researcher observes: aid was followed by growth. But the recovery would have happened anyway.




Extreme observations tend to move back toward the long-run average over time
If bad growth attracts aid, and bad growth predicts recovery, you get a spurious positive correlation
CRBB test: controlling for lagged growth does not change the results

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
US Aid Has Collapsed



The US is historically the world’s largest bilateral donor
In early 2025, the Trump administration dismantled USAID and froze most foreign assistance
Dozens of countries lost their primary external funding source within weeks

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Why Should Aid Raise Growth?


Savings gap: poor countries have low income, low savings, low investment. Aid injects foreign capital to break the cycle.
Big push: some investments only pay off if many happen simultaneously. A road without trucks, fuel, and mechanics is useless. Aid can coordinate.
Public goods: markets will not build courts, property registries, or basic health infrastructure. Aid can finance what no private actor will.
Shock buffer: a drought or conflict can destroy years of accumulated capital. Aid prevents temporary setbacks from becoming permanent traps.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Fungibility
The government receives $100 million earmarked for schools. Does education spending rise by $100 million?


Not necessarily. The government can reduce its own education budget by $80 million, spending the freed-up money elsewhere.
Feyzioglu et al. (1998): on average, $1 of sectoral aid raises sector spending by roughly $0.25.
Reinikka & Svensson (2004) tracked education grants to Ugandan schools in the 1990s: 13 cents of every dollar reached the school. The rest was captured at district and local levels.



Fungibility does not mean aid is worthless, but it means the effective dose is much smaller than the nominal transfer.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Dutch Disease


Any large foreign inflow appreciates the local currency
Imports become cheap; exports become expensive on world markets
Manufacturing and agriculture contract, even when the aid itself is well-spent
The economy shifts toward non-tradables: construction, services, government

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Corruption and Leakage


Aid passes through many hands before reaching its destination: central government, line ministries, local officials, contractors
At each step, there are opportunities for diversion
Weak procurement systems, poor auditing, and political pressure all amplify leakage
This does not mean aid always fails, but it reduces the expected return sharply when institutions are weak
The countries most in need of aid are often those with the weakest institutions

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
The Accountability Problem


A government funded by taxes is accountable to taxpayers: fail to deliver and you lose revenue and legitimacy
A government funded primarily by donors is accountable to donors, not citizens
Citizens have less leverage when the state does not depend on their compliance
Donors care about disbursement targets and project metrics, not long-run development outcomes



Briggs (2021) surveyed World Bank task team leaders. Career advancement depended on getting projects approved and implemented, not on whether they reached the poorest. Incentives shape where aid actually goes.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Where Does Aid Actually Go?


Donors say aid targets the poorest. But within recipient countries, does it?
Briggs (2016): multilateral aid projects are systematically directed toward middle-income regions, not the poorest subnational areas
Recipient governments push aid toward politically connected areas; donors need implementable projects, which are harder in remote, poor regions
The stated goal (poverty reduction) and the actual allocation diverge because of political economy on both sides

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
So Does Aid Cause Growth?


Burnside & Dollar (2000): yes, but only with good fiscal and trade policy
Rajan & Subramanian (2008): no robust effect, even conditional on good policy
Hansen & Tarp (2001): positive but with strong diminishing returns
Micro-level evaluations: often positive for specific, targeted programs

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
CRBB: Two Fixable Problems


These studies overlap substantially in countries, years, and data sources
CRBB argue the divergence comes from two resolvable research design choices
The first is about measurement: what counts as aid, and over what time horizon?
The second is about identification: how do you separate the effect of aid from the effect of everything that moves with aid?

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Aid as a Windfall
Your government receives $500 million from abroad: no goods produced, arrives every year.

Think of it like oil revenue or winning the lottery at the country level.




Does it foster development?
Does it crowd out domestic effort?
Does it change who the government is accountable to?

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Why a Windfall Should Help
Poor countries are caught in a trap: low income means low savings, low savings means low investment, low investment means slow growth.


Savings gap: external capital breaks the trap by funding investment that domestic savings cannot
Public goods: markets won’t build courts, property registries, or power grids. Aid can.
Big push: some investments only work if many happen at once. A road needs trucks, fuel, mechanics. Aid can coordinate.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Does the Windfall Actually Arrive?
You earmark $100 million for schools. Does education spending rise by $100 million?


Not necessarily. The government cuts its own education budget by $80 million.
The windfall frees up domestic resources that go elsewhere.
Reinikka & Svensson (2004): in Uganda, 13 cents per dollar of education grants reached the school.



This is fungibility. The effective dose is much smaller than the nominal transfer.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Does the Windfall Hurt Exporters?


Large inflows raise demand for local goods: construction, real estate, services
Local prices rise; the real exchange rate appreciates
Exports become expensive internationally; manufacturing and agriculture contract



Dutch disease. Named for the Netherlands after North Sea gas was discovered in the 1960s: manufacturing contracted as the guilder appreciated. Same mechanism, any unearned windfall.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
section: Does the Windfall Reach the Right People?
text:
Does the Windfall Reach the Right People?


Aid passes through many hands: central government, ministries, local officials, contractors
Leakage at every step. The countries most in need often have the weakest institutions.
Briggs (2016): within recipient countries, multilateral aid goes to middle-income regions, not the poorest. Donor career incentives and recipient politics both push in that direction.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
section: Does the Windfall Change Who Governs For Whom?
text:
Does the Windfall Change Who Governs For Whom?
A government that depends on taxes is accountable to taxpayers. What about a government that depends on donors?


Citizens have less leverage when the state does not need their compliance or their money
Donors care about disbursement targets and project metrics, not long-run development
Briggs (2021): World Bank task team leaders face career pressure to get projects approved and implemented, not to reach the poorest
Aid can weaken the fiscal contract between state and society

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Two Fixable Problems


CRBB argue the divergence comes from two resolvable research design choices
Measurement: what counts as development aid, and over what time horizon?
Identification: how do you separate the effect of aid from the effect of everything that moves with aid?

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Decision 2: Which Aid Flows?
Your data includes roads, food relief, vaccination campaigns, budget support, technical cooperation.


(a) All disbursements: most flows have no short-run growth mechanism. Testing noise.
(b) Project aid only: misses budget support, which can fund productive investment.
(c) Early-impact only: aid that could plausibly raise productive capacity in a few years.



CRBB choose (c). About 45 to 53% of total flows.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Aid and Accountability
A government that depends on taxes is accountable to taxpayers. What about a government that depends on donors?


Citizens have less leverage when the state does not need their compliance or money
Donors care about disbursement targets and project metrics, not long-run development
Briggs (2021): World Bank task team leaders face career pressure to get projects approved, not to reach the poorest



Aid can weaken the fiscal contract between state and society.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
The Evidence Is Mixed
The macro cross-country results span from “strongly positive” to “no effect,” using similar data and periods.

Is the disagreement real heterogeneity — aid works in some places but not others? Or a measurement problem?


That is what CRBB ask.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
What Is First-Differencing?
Country fixed effects absorb the country mean: \[y_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta \,\text{Aid}_{i,t-1} + \epsilon_{it}\]

First-differencing subtracts last period’s values — \(\alpha_i\) appears in both and cancels: \[\Delta y_{it} = \beta \,\Delta\text{Aid}_{i,t-1} + \Delta\epsilon_{it}\]


FE: was Nigeria richer than its own average in years when it got more aid?
FD: did Nigeria grow faster than last period when it got more aid than last period?
CRBB use FD. It controls for country fixed effects algebraically — no need to add country dummies separately.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text: Mean Reversion

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
If Used Well


Savings gap: external capital breaks the low-income → low-savings → low-investment cycle
Public goods: courts, roads, power grids; markets won’t build them
Big push: some investments only pay off if many happen at once; aid can coordinate

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Even If Used Well


Dutch disease: large inflows appreciate the currency, making exports expensive and contracting manufacturing
Accountability shift: a government funded by donors answers to donors, not citizens

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
If Used Poorly


Fungibility: aid frees up domestic funds already earmarked for the same thing. Reinikka & Svensson (2004): 13 cents per dollar reached Ugandan schools
Corruption: aid passes through many hands; weak institutions mean diversion at every step
Misallocation: Briggs (2016): multilateral aid within countries flows to middle-income regions, not the poorest

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Empirically: What Happens?


Burnside & Dollar (2000): positive, but only with good policy — consistent with “used well” mattering
Rajan & Subramanian (2008): no robust effect — consistent with average inefficiency dominating
Hansen & Tarp (2001): positive but diminishing — consistent with absorption limits
Micro-level RCTs: often positive for specific, well-targeted programs



The macro evidence is mixed. Is this real heterogeneity, or a measurement problem? That is what CRBB ask.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
section: Research Design Is Not a Formality
text:
Research Design Is Not a Formality
Three studies. Similar data. Three different answers. The differences came from measurement and identification choices.


What you measure: aggregate aid vs. early-impact aid
When you measure: contemporaneous vs. lagged
How you identify: invalid instruments vs. first-differencing



Every design choice either makes a null result informative or stacks the deck against finding an effect. Think through and justify each one: what unit, what measure, what time window, what comparison group.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Mean Reversion in Aid Research
Very tall parents tend to have tall children, but pulled toward the average. The same logic applies to country growth.


A country has a terrible growth year. Donors respond with more aid.
The next period, growth recovers — partly because bad years do not persist.
A researcher observes: aid was followed by growth.
But the recovery may have happened regardless.



A researcher observing this pattern cannot tell whether aid caused the recovery or whether the recovery was coming anyway.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Fixed Effects vs. First-Differencing
Both remove time-invariant country traits (\(\alpha_i\) cancels in both). The difference is what question they answer.

Country FE — deviation from the country’s long-run mean: \[y_{it} - \bar{y}_i = \beta(\text{Aid}_{i,t-1} - \overline{\text{Aid}}_i) + \ldots\] Was Nigeria above its own average when it got more aid than usual?


First-difference — change from the previous period: \[\Delta y_{it} = \beta \,\Delta\text{Aid}_{i,t-1} + \ldots\] Did Nigeria grow faster this period than last when aid increased?


FD is stricter: it also removes slow-moving country trends, not just the long-run mean.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
FE vs. First-Differencing


Country FE: deviation from country long-run mean; was Nigeria above its own average when aid was higher? \[y_{it} - \bar{y}_i = \beta(\text{Aid}_{i,t-1} - \overline{\text{Aid}}_i)\]
First-difference: change from previous period; did Nigeria grow faster when aid increased? \[\Delta y_{it} = \beta \,\Delta\text{Aid}_{i,t-1}\]
FD looks at period-to-period changes

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Empirical Evidence


Burnside & Dollar (2000): positive, but only with good policy
Rajan & Subramanian (2008): no robust effect, even with good policy
Hansen & Tarp (2001): positive but diminishing returns
Micro-level RCTs: often positive for specific, well-targeted programs



The macro evidence is mixed. Is this real heterogeneity, or a measurement problem?

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Time Horizon


A road raises productivity for decades; food relief addresses a crisis this week
Testing whether all aid raises GDP this year is asking whether food relief builds roads
The time horizon should depend on what type of aid you are measuring

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Aid Types


Early-impact: budget support, roads, energy, agriculture; plausible growth effect within a few years
Long-horizon: education, health, technical cooperation; growth effects arrive over a generation
No clear growth mechanism: humanitarian aid, food relief, emergency assistance

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Decision 1: Lag
We receive aid in t - when should we measure development?


(a) Same period: potential reverse causation
(b) Next period: allows time for aid to work
(c) Much longer: plausible for infrastructure, but a lot of things change



CRBB choose (b): does Aid(\(t-1\)) predict Growth(\(t\))?

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Decision 2: Aid
What type aid should spur development?


(a) All disbursements: food relief, technical assistance, emergency aid, budget support, infrastructure; everything in the data
(b) Project aid: tied to specific outputs; excludes budget support, which can also fund productive investment
(c) Early-impact only: budget support, roads, energy, agriculture; roughly 45-53% of total flows



CRBB choose (c)

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
The Causal Problem
Even with the right measure and the right lag, a problem remains.


Countries that receive more aid tend to be poorer and slower-growing
Aid and low growth travel together in the data
Is aid causing slow growth, or is slow growth causing more aid?

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Decision 3: Confounders
Poor, conflict-prone countries attract more aid and grow more slowly.

The problem: geography, colonial history, institutions, conflict all affect both aid receipt and growth; none of these are caused by aid

Design Choices
Three studies, similar data, three different answers: the divergence came from measurement and identification choices.


What you measure: aggregate aid vs. early-impact aid
When you measure: contemporaneous vs. lagged
How you identify: name the source of clean variation and defend why it is not driven by outcomes



Every design choice either makes a null result informative or stacks the deck against finding one.

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Econ 101: For


Poor countries are caught in a trap: low income → low savings → low investment → low income
Aid injects foreign capital and breaks the cycle
In capital-scarce economies, returns to investment are high; well-deployed aid can go far

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Poli Sci 101: For


Poor governments often cannot fund public goods: courts, schools, clinics
Markets won’t provide them; no one can exclude free riders
Aid can solve collective action problems no domestic actor will fund unilaterally
Big push: some investments only pay off if many happen at once; aid coordinates

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Poli Sci 101: Against


A government funded by donors answers to donors, not citizens
If aid makes governments less reliant on taxation → less representation; citizens lose leverage over the state
Aid creates rents worth capturing: incentives to divert and steal

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
The Counterfactual


Question: does aid produce development in recipient countries, relative to development had they not received aid?
Empirically tough to answer! Aid goes to poorer, slower-growing countries and those in crisis

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
What Is the Goal?


Development: Reduce global poverty
Humanitarian: Relief during crisis and disasters
Strategic: geopolitical influence, commercial access?

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Does aid foster development?
Your government receives $500 million from abroad

Does it spur development, and if so, why?

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Econ 101: The case for “Yes”


Poor countries are caught in a trap: low income → low savings → low investment → low income
Aid injects foreign capital and breaks the cycle
In capital-scarce economies, returns to investment are high

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Econ 101: The case for “Maybe”


Any large foreign inflow appreciates the local currency
Imports become cheap; exports become expensive on world markets
Manufacturing and agriculture contract

title: Foreign Aid and Development
text:
Poli Sci 101: The case for “Yes”


Poor governments often cannot fund public goods: courts, schools, clinics
Politicians have short-term incentives, investment in public goods requires longer time horizons
Aid can fund investments with long time horizons that short electoral cycles make unattractive

title: Education and Development
text:
The Big Claim


Education is often called the highest-return investment in development
Girls’ schooling has been linked to lower fertility, lower child mortality, higher incomes
Cross-country: years of schooling correlates strongly with GDP per capita
Is this causal, or is it the selection story all over again?

title: Education and Development
text:
Schooling Has Exploded


1950: average adult in low-income countries had ~2 years of schooling
2020: average adult has ~7 years
Primary enrollment in sub-Saharan Africa: 52% in 1970, 98% by 2015
Gains are largest among girls and in the poorest countries

title: Education and Development
text:
But Learning Has Not


More years in school do not automatically mean more learning
In rural India, ~50% of grade 5 students cannot read a grade 2 text
In many low-income countries, grade 3 students cannot do single-digit subtraction
The “learning crisis”: enrollment up, skills flat

title: Education and Development
text:
Why Might Education Pay?


Human capital (Becker): school builds productive skills; higher skill → higher wages
Signaling (Spence, 1973): school reveals underlying ability to employers
Both predict: more school → higher wages
They disagree on why, and on what policy should do

title: Education and Development
text:
Becker: Skills


Workers choose schooling like an investment
Costs: tuition, forgone earnings
Returns: higher productivity, higher wages over lifetime
Implication: expanding schools should raise wages, because new skills are being built

title: Education and Development
text:
Spence: Signals


Ability is unobservable to employers at hiring
High-ability workers find school cheap; low-ability workers find it costly
A diploma separates types even if the content is useless
Implication: expanding schools may not raise wages if it only shifts the signal

title: Education and Development
text:
Why the Distinction Matters


Human capital: policy should build more schools, train more teachers
Signaling: policy should fund only the credential, or find cheaper signals
Most evidence suggests both are at play; pure signaling is rare
Testing them requires variation that breaks the ability-schooling link

title: Education and Development
text:
OLS Returns to Schooling
\[\ln(\text{wage}_i) = \alpha + \beta \cdot \text{school}_i + \varepsilon_i\]


Typical OLS estimate: \(\hat\beta \approx 0.08\) to \(0.10\)
Interpretation: one more year of school is associated with 8-10% higher wages
“Associated with”, not “causes”

title: Education and Development
text:
Ability Bias


High-ability people get more schooling AND earn more
OLS attributes the full wage gap to schooling
True causal effect is smaller than the correlation
Classic upward bias

title: Education and Development
text:
Reverse Causation and Selection


Richer families can afford more schooling; their kids also inherit networks, health, nutrition
Poor regions have worse schools AND worse labor markets
Any observed correlation mixes all of these
We need exogenous variation in schooling

title: Education and Development
text:
Classic Fixes


Twins studies: compare siblings to hold genes constant
Compulsory schooling laws: use legal cutoffs as a shock
Both mostly come from rich countries
Do they apply in low-income settings where access, not motivation, is the bind?

title: Education and Development
text:
The Setup


Some units get treated; others do not
We observe outcomes before and after
Simple comparison of treated post-treatment is confounded by unit differences
Simple before-after on treated is confounded by time trends

title: Education and Development
text:
The 2×2 Table




Before
After




Treated
\(Y_{T,0}\)
\(Y_{T,1}\)


Control
\(Y_{C,0}\)
\(Y_{C,1}\)




\[\hat\delta_{DiD} = (Y_{T,1} - Y_{T,0}) - (Y_{C,1} - Y_{C,0})\]

title: Education and Development
text:
What DiD Assumes


Parallel trends: without treatment, treated and control would have evolved the same way
Unit fixed effects absorb any time-invariant differences
Time fixed effects absorb any common shocks
The treatment effect lives in the interaction

title: Education and Development
text:
DiD as a Regression
\[Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \delta (\text{Treated}_i \times \text{Post}_t) + \varepsilon_{it}\]


\(\alpha_i\): unit fixed effects (absorbs level differences)
\(\lambda_t\): time fixed effects (absorbs common trends)
\(\delta\): coefficient on the interaction = DiD estimate
DiD is an interaction term, nothing more

title: Education and Development
text:
Why This Matters Today


Duflo (2001) uses a continuous DiD: intensity of treatment × exposure cohort
The interaction of how much treatment and who was exposed is the instrument
Same logic, more variation

title: Education and Development
text:
The Setting


Indonesia, early 1970s: primary enrollment ~60%, large regional gaps
1973 oil windfall funds a massive public investment
1973-1978: INPRES program builds 61,807 primary schools
Roughly doubles the existing stock in five years

title: Education and Development
text:
The Allocation Rule


Schools allocated across 283 regions
Rule: more schools to regions with fewer existing schools per child
Program intensity = schools built per 1,000 children in region
Not random, but driven by a formula, not local demand

title: Education and Development
text:
Two Dimensions of Variation


Region: some regions got more schools (high intensity)
Cohort: some children were young enough to benefit, others had already finished primary school
Children aged 2-6 in 1974: fully exposed
Children aged 12+ in 1974: already past primary

title: Education and Development
text:
The Design


High-intensity region + young cohort = most treatment
Low-intensity region + old cohort = no treatment
Compare the difference across cohorts in high vs low-intensity regions
Continuous DiD: intensity × exposure

title: Education and Development
text:
The Identifying Assumption


Without INPRES, young cohorts in high-intensity regions would have evolved like young cohorts in low-intensity regions
Threat: maybe high-intensity regions were catching up for other reasons
Test: look at cohorts too old to be treated
If their education rises with intensity, parallel trends fails

title: Education and Development
text:
Placebo Cohorts


Compare ages 12-17 vs ages 18-24 in 1974
Neither group was exposed to INPRES schools
If intensity predicts differences between these cohorts, we have a problem
It does not; the effect turns on precisely at age 12

title: Education and Development
text:
First Stage: Education


One more school per 1,000 children → 0.12 to 0.19 more years of schooling
Effect concentrated at primary completion, not secondary
Larger in sparser, poorer regions (where the constraint was bindings)
Consistent with supply-side access story

title: Education and Development
text:
Reduced Form: Wages


One more school per 1,000 children → 1.5% to 2.7% higher adult wages
Same cohort × intensity interaction, now on earnings
Estimated in 1995, ~20 years after exposure

title: Education and Development
text:
From DiD to IV


First stage: intensity × exposure → more schooling
Reduced form: intensity × exposure → higher wages
Ratio: wage effect per year of schooling
This is 2SLS: the interaction is an instrument for education

title: Education and Development
text:
2SLS Returns


Returns to education: 6.8% to 10.6% per year
OLS returns in the same data: ~7.5%
In this setting, OLS is not wildly biased
But the IV estimate is a LATE, not an average

title: Education and Development
text:
LATE Interpretation


2SLS identifies the return for compliers: students induced to attend by the new schools
These are children who would not have gone without INPRES
Likely poorer, more rural, more credit-constrained
Their return need not equal the return for infra-marginal students

title: Education and Development
text:
Cost-Benefit


Cost per school: ~$24,300 in 1990 USD
Implied internal rate of return: 8.8% to 12%
Competitive with returns to physical capital
Supply-side education investment paid for itself

title: Education and Development
text:
What to Take Away


Access, not just demand, was a real constraint in 1970s Indonesia
A continuous DiD with an interaction instrument isolates causal returns
Returns to schooling are positive and economically meaningful
Human capital story wins here; pure signaling cannot explain wage gains from building more schools

title: Education and Development
text:
Limitations


LATE: results apply to compliers, not everyone
Indonesia in 1995: formal-sector wages, not informal or agricultural
Primary schooling, not secondary or tertiary
Learning crisis literature suggests building schools today may not pay the same return

title: Education and Development
text:
What Education Economics Teaches


Education correlates with development, but correlation is not causation
Credible designs turn on variation that breaks the ability-schooling link
Duflo (2001): supply-side shocks + DiD + IV = a clean answer
The learning crisis is the open frontier: years of school are rising; skills are not
